# Introduction to NoSQL Databases

MongoDB is one member of a broader family of non-relational database technologies

<!--
The slide title is: Introduction to NoSQL Databases.

The slide says: MongoDB is one member of a broader family of non-relational database technologies.
-->

---































<!-- _class: content -->

# Module Learning Objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to:

- Define NoSQL as a category, not one product
- Compare document, key-value, column-family, and graph models
- Explain MongoDB documents, collections, and BSON
- Describe the basic MongoDB architecture
- Select workloads that are — and are not — good MongoDB candidates

<!-- _class: split -->

# Structured vs Semi-Structured vs Unstructured

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Structured:** rows and columns with a declared schema
- **Semi-structured:** nested JSON-like records; fields can vary
- **Unstructured:** images, logs, and media with no field layout

MongoDB is strongest on **semi-structured, hierarchical** application data.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/02-structured-semi-unstructured.svg" alt="Side-by-side structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Where Relational Databases Work Well

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Structured, predictable schemas
- Strong relationships between tables
- Complex multi-table transactions
- Mature SQL reporting
- Financial and accounting systems

**Key message:** NoSQL is not a universal replacement for relational databases.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/03-relational-database-model.svg" alt="Application connected to normalized tables with keys and relationships" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Challenges with Traditional Relational Models

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Rigid schemas and frequent migrations
- Complex joins to rebuild one object
- Object-relational mapping overhead
- Horizontal scaling is harder than one server
- Many tables for one business object

**Example:** `customers` · `addresses` · `orders` · `order_items` · `payments`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/04-relational-data-challenges.svg" alt="One order reconstructed by joining many tables" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# What Does NoSQL Mean?

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

NoSQL commonly means **“Not Only SQL.”**

- Flexible or non-tabular models
- Horizontal scaling and availability
- Application-oriented schemas

**Key message:** NoSQL is a category, not one standard technology.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/06-sql-vs-nosql.svg" alt="SQL versus NoSQL comparison of schema, storage, relationships, scaling" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# The Four Major NoSQL Database Types

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

| Type | Primary structure |
|------|-------------------|
| Document | JSON-like documents |
| Key-value | Key mapped to a value |
| Column-family | Rows with flexible columns |
| Graph | Nodes and relationships |

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/07-nosql-database-landscape.svg" alt="Four NoSQL branches: document, key-value, column-family, graph" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Document Databases

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Database → collection → document
- Fields, nested objects, arrays
- Natural application objects
- Flexible fields; fewer joins for many reads

**Examples:** MongoDB, Couchbase

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/08-document-database-model.svg" alt="Collection of JSON-like documents with fields, arrays, and nested objects" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Key-Value Databases

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

**Structure:** `Key → Value`

- Sessions, caching, carts
- Fast lookup by a known key
- Querying *inside* the value may be limited

**Example:** Redis

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/09-key-value-database-model.svg" alt="Session and cart keys mapped directly to values" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Column-Family Databases

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Rows with flexible columns
- Grouped into column families
- Built for large distributed writes

**Use cases:** telemetry, events, time-series ingest

**Examples:** Cassandra, HBase

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/10-column-family-database-model.svg" alt="Flexible rows organized into column families" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Graph Databases

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Nodes** = entities
- **Edges** = relationships
- **Properties** describe both

**Use cases:** fraud, social, recommendations

**Example:** Neo4j

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/11-graph-database-model.svg" alt="Customers, products, and purchases as nodes and relationships" width="720">

# Choosing the Right Database Model

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Begin with access patterns, consistency, relationships, and scale.

| Scenario | Model |
|----------|-------|
| Session lookup | Key-value |
| Product catalog | Document |
| Social graph | Graph |
| Telemetry ingest | Column-family |
| Financial ledger | Relational |

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/12-nosql-model-comparison.svg" alt="Four-way comparison of structure, access pattern, and use case" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Database Selection Decision Flow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Ask, in order:

1. Are **paths** the query?
2. Is it a **direct key lookup**?
3. Are **attributes varied** and nested?
4. Are **multi-table transactions** mandatory?
5. Is the load **massive distributed writes**?

Then pick a **product** inside that model.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/13-database-selection-decision-flow.svg" alt="Decision flow from workload need to database model" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# MongoDB Data Hierarchy

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Server hosts one or more **databases**
- A database holds **collections**
- A collection holds **documents**
- A document holds **fields**, nested objects, and arrays

This is the map for Lab 1.3: `show dbs` → `use` → `show collections` → `findOne`.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/15-mongodb-data-hierarchy.svg" alt="MongoDB server to database to collection to document to field" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

# Embedding vs Referencing Preview

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Embed** when you read it together
- **Reference** when it is shared or must stay current
- Purchase-time **price** is a snapshot — embed it

Module 3 goes deeper. Here: notice the choice exists.

</div>

</div>
</div>

# MongoDB Architecture Overview

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Client application
- MongoDB driver
- MongoDB server
- Database → collection → document
- Storage engine
- Indexes

Replication and sharding: high level only. **Module 7** covers them.

</div>

# How a MongoDB Request Is Processed

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

```javascript
db.products.find({ category: "Accessories" })
```

1. Application sends the query through a driver
2. Server parses and plans the query
3. MongoDB checks available indexes
4. Storage engine retrieves matches
5. Results return to the application

**Key message:** Query design, schema design, and indexing work together.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/23-mongodb-request-flow.svg" alt="Query through driver, planner, index, storage engine, and results" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Core MongoDB Features

<div class="cols">

- Query language and aggregation
- Indexes and transactions
- Replica sets and sharding
- Drivers and access control

# When to Use MongoDB

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Choose MongoDB when data is:

- Hierarchical and application-centered
- Varied across records
- Changing as features ship
- Already JSON in the API

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/27-when-to-use-mongodb.svg" alt="When MongoDB fits: flexible hierarchical application data" width="720">

# When MongoDB May Not Be the Best Choice

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Wrong *first* choice when:

- Complex relational reporting
- Specialized graph traversal
- Cache-only lookup
- SQL-only tools are mandatory

**Key message:** Fit the workload, not the trend.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-01/28-when-mongodb-may-not-fit.svg" alt="When MongoDB is a weak first choice" width="720">

- **Expected:** All six rows of the deliverable table are filled. You can explain why another technology might also work, and why your first choice still fits.

## Exercise 1.2 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 1.2`](../slide-exercises/module-01/exercise-1.2-rows-to-documents.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Read the three relational tables**
- **Do:** Identify how you would reconstruct one complete order in SQL: join `Customer` to `Order` on `customer_id`, then join `Order items` on `order_id`. List every field the application needs for “show order O5001.”
- **Expected:** You can name the three tables and the join keys. You know the order total is 110.00 and there are two line items.

**Step 2 — Draft one JSON-like order document**
- **Do:** Create a single document that holds the order header. Do not worry about `_id` or nesting yet — get `status` and `total` on the page.
- **Expected:** A starting object exists, for example `{ orderId: "O5001", status: "PLACED", total: 110.00 }`.

**Step 3 — Embed items, customer, and `_id`**
- **Do:** Embed the two order items as an array. Include essential customer information (id, name, email). Set `_id` to `"O5001"` (or an ObjectId if you prefer). Keep purchase-time `price` on each item.
- **Expected:** One document that looks like the solution below: `_id`, nested `customer`, `items` array, `status`, and `total`. You did not leave items in a separate table.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

## Exercise 1.2 — Steps 3–4

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 1.2`](../slide-exercises/module-01/exercise-1.2-rows-to-documents.md)
**Step 3 — Embed items, customer, and `_id`**
- **Do:** Embed two items as an array, include customer id/name/email, set `_id` to `"O5001"`, keep purchase-time price on each item.
- **Expected:** One document — not a document per line item.

**Step 4 — Identify snapshot versus stale fields**
- **Do:** Decide email embed vs reference, purchase-time vs current price, and the main query this document supports.
- **Expected:** Price is a snapshot; email can go stale; the shape serves “get order O5001 in one read.”

## Exercise 1.3 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 1.3`](../slide-exercises/module-01/exercise-1.3-explore-a-mongodb-dataset.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — View available databases**
- **Do:** In `mongosh`, run: javascript show dbs
- **Expected:** The database list includes `training_store` (and usually `admin`, `config`, and `local`).

**Step 2 — Select the training database and list collections**
- **Do:** Run: javascript use training_store show collections
- **Expected:** The prompt shows `training_store`. Collections include `customers`, `products`, and `orders`.

**Step 3 — Retrieve one product document**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.findOne()
- **Expected:** One product document prints. You can see `_id`, scalar fields such as `name` and `price`, and at least one nested or category-specific field.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

# MongoDB Installation and Setup

Before documents and queries: a reliable environment and a verified client connection

<!--
The slide title is: MongoDB Installation and Setup.

<!-- _class: content -->

# Module Learning Objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to:

- Choose local, self-managed, container, or managed-cloud MongoDB
- Identify server, clients, configuration, data, and logs
- Install or provision an instance and verify it is running
- Connect with `mongosh` and MongoDB Compass
- Interpret a connection string
- Create a database and collection; insert and retrieve a test document
- Apply basic credential and network hygiene
- Diagnose common install and connectivity failures

# MongoDB Environment Components

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Server (`mongod`):** stores and processes data
- **Shell (`mongosh`):** command-line client
- **Compass:** graphical client
- **Driver:** application connectivity
- **Configuration:** ports, paths, security
- **Data files and logs:** persistence and diagnostics

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/01-environment-overview.svg" alt="Developer to clients to MongoDB server to database files" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Environment Layers

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

A failure can sit at any layer:

- Client tools
- Network
- Server process
- Storage engine
- Data and indexes

**Key message:** “MongoDB is installed” is not the same as “I can write a document.”

</div>

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `mongod` server process
- Command-line tools
- Configuration file
- Data directory
- Log directory

# Managed Cloud Deployment

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Typical provisioning:

1. Sign in and select a project
2. Create a database deployment
3. Create a database user
4. Configure network access
5. Copy the connection string
6. Connect with `mongosh`, Compass, or a driver

**Key message:** A user and an allowed network source are required before connecting.

</div>

# Self-Managed Server

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Client on the organizational network
- MongoDB on a server or VM you control
- Attached storage you back up
- Patches, firewall, and DNS are yours

**Best fit:** regulated environments that require direct infrastructure control.

</div>

# Local vs. Managed Cloud

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

**Key message:** The database commands are largely similar. Infrastructure responsibility differs.

Local: you install, patch, and back up.

Cloud: you still create a user, allow a network, and protect the URI.

</div>

<div class="cols">

# MongoDB Server and Client Tools

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| `mongod` | Database **server** |
| `mongosh` | Command-line **client** |
| Compass | Graphical **client** |
| Driver | Application connectivity |
| Database tools | Import, export, backup |

**Misconception:** `mongosh` is not the database server.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/10-server-and-client-tools.svg" alt="mongod in the center connected to mongosh, Compass, driver, and tools" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# `mongod` vs. `mongosh`

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

`mongod` accepts connections, processes operations, manages files and indexes, writes logs, and enforces configured security.

`mongosh` sends commands and prints results.

```text
mongod  = server
mongosh = client
```

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/11-mongod-vs-mongosh.svg" alt="Side-by-side mongod server responsibilities versus mongosh client" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Three Clients, One Deployment

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Shell, Compass, and an application driver all target the **same** MongoDB.

They are different interfaces, not different databases.

Drivers show up again in Module 8.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/12-client-connection-options.svg" alt="mongosh, Compass, and driver converging on one deployment" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# MongoDB Configuration File

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Common categories:

- Storage / `dbPath`
- Logging
- Network (`port`, `bindIp`)
- Security
- Replication
- Process management

**Security:** Do not broaden `bindIp` without authentication and network controls.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/16-configuration-map.svg" alt="Config file branching into storage, logging, network, security, replication, process" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Logging.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Network (port, bindIp).

Bullet 4 on the slide: Security.

Bullet 5 on the slide: Replication.

Bullet 6 on the slide: Process management.

<!-- _class: split -->

# Data and Log Directories

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

**Data directory:** collections, indexes, storage-engine files, metadata.

**Log directory:** startup, connections, warnings, authentication failures, config errors, shutdown.

**Troubleshooting:** If the server fails to start, inspect the server log.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/15-file-system-components.svg" alt="mongod process using config file, data directory, and log directory" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Data and Log Flow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

A client operation is executed by the server.

- Successful writes land in **data files**
- Operational events land in **log files**

You do not need `mongosh` to diagnose a startup failure.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/17-data-and-log-flow.svg" alt="Client operation to server, then to data files and log files" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: Operational events land in log files.

# Starting and Stopping MongoDB

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Depends on the environment:

- Operating-system service
- Manual `mongod` process
- Container start / stop
- Managed-cloud control plane

Stop **gracefully**. Confirm state. Avoid force-kill unless recovering.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/21-os-service-lifecycle.svg" alt="Install, register, start, running, stop, restart" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Startup and Shutdown

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

**Start:** read config → validate paths → open port → initialize storage → accept connections.

**Stop:** finish operations → flush data → close files → stop service.

A kill can force recovery on the next start.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/22-startup-sequence.svg" alt="MongoDB startup sequence from configuration to accepting connections" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Verifying the MongoDB Service

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

1. Process running?
2. Port listening?
3. Client can reach?
4. Authentication succeeds?
5. A command works?
6. Write and read?

```javascript
db.runCommand({ ping: 1 })
```

Success includes `ok: 1`. Ping is **not** a write test.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/24-environment-readiness-flow.svg" alt="Readiness questions from server running through read/write" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Hosts and Ports

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

**Default local:** `localhost` · port **27017**

Also: hostname, IP, network interface, firewall, DNS, allowlist.

**Important:** A running database may still be unreachable.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

# Localhost vs. Remote Connection

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Same workstation: `mongodb://localhost:27017`

Remote: client → network → firewall → host → database.

Cloud adds TLS and an IP allowlist.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/26-localhost-connection.svg" alt="mongosh and mongod on the same workstation via localhost 27017" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Understanding Connection Strings

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

A URI tells the client:

- Protocol
- Host or cluster
- Port
- Credentials
- Default database
- Options

```text
mongodb://username:password@host:port/database
```

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/31-connection-string-anatomy.svg" alt="Labeled protocol, username, password, host, port, database, options" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Standard Connection-String Format

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

```text
mongodb://[username:password@]host[:port]/[database][?options]
```

Local:

```text
mongodb://localhost:27017
```

Authenticated (placeholder):

```text
mongodb://appuser:password@dbhost:27017/training
```

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/32-standard-mongodb-uri.svg" alt="Visual breakdown of mongodb://username:password@host:27017/database" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The slide says: Local:.

The slide says: </div>.

The figure on this slide is titled: Visual breakdown of mongodb://username:password@host:27017/database.

The code on the slide reads: mongodb://[username:password@]host[:port]/[database][?options].

The code on the slide reads: mongodb://localhost:27017.

The code on the slide reads: mongodb://appuser:password@dbhost:27017/training.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# DNS Seed-List Connection Strings

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

```text
mongodb+srv://username:password@cluster-host/database
```

- Uses DNS to discover members
- Common for managed services
- Port often omitted

```text
mongodb://
mongodb+srv://
```

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/34-mongodb-vs-mongodb-srv.svg" alt="Direct host-and-port URI compared with DNS seed-list URI" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Connection Establishment

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

1. Parse URI
2. Resolve host
3. Network connection
4. Negotiate TLS
5. Authenticate
6. Select database

The error message usually names the step that failed.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/35-connection-establishment-sequence.svg" alt="Parse URI through authenticate and select database" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 2.2 — Steps 1–2

**Step 1 — Label the connection-string parts**
- **Do:** Using this sample, identify protocol, username, password placeholder, host, port, and default database: text mongodb://trainingUser:password@db.example.net:27017/training
- **Expected:** Your notes name all six parts. You can point to where each value sits in the URI.

**Step 2 — Answer the security questions**
- **Do:** Write a short answer for each: 1. Which part must not appear in a screenshot? 2. Which values should be stored securely? 3. What could cause this connection to fail? 4. How should the password be supplied in a real appli
- **Expected:** You refuse to put the password in slides or source. You can name at least two failure causes (wrong password, host unreachable, port, DNS, TLS).

**Step 3 — Compare `mongodb://` and `mongodb+srv://`**
- **Do:** Write one sentence for each scheme. Note which form managed-cloud services commonly provide.
- **Expected:** You can say that `mongodb://` lists hosts (and optional port) and `mongodb+srv://` uses DNS to discover deployment information.

```javascript
db
```

# Creating Your First Database

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

```javascript
use training_store
db
```

Selecting a database does **not** always persist it immediately.

It normally becomes visible in `show dbs` after data is stored.

</div>

# Creating Your First Collection

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

**Explicit**

```javascript
db.createCollection("products")
```

**Implicit** — first insert creates the collection.

Use explicit creation when options or validation matter.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/43-explicit-vs-implicit-collection.svg" alt="createCollection versus collection created on first insert" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Inserting Your First Document

# Automatic `_id` Generation

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

If you omit `_id`, MongoDB assigns a unique **ObjectId**.

That identifier is how Compass and `findOne` locate the same document.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/45-automatic-id-generation.svg" alt="Document without _id stored with generated ObjectId" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Retrieving and Verifying Data

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

```javascript
db.products.findOne()
db.products.findOne({ sku: "P1001" })
db.products.countDocuments({})
```

**Principle:** Prove the install with a **write and a read**. Ping only proves reachability.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

</div>
</div>

# Same Data Through Two Clients

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

`mongosh` inserts. MongoDB stores. Compass displays.

If Compass cannot see the insert, you are on a different URI, user, or database.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/49-same-data-two-clients.svg" alt="mongosh insert stored by MongoDB and shown in Compass" width="720">

# Basic Authentication Concepts

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Database user, password, authentication database
- Roles and least privilege
- Network authorization (who may even try)

**Authentication:** Who are you?

**Authorization:** What may you do?

Detailed security is Module 8.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/50-authentication-vs-authorization.svg" alt="Authentication who are you versus authorization what may you do" width="720">

# Layered Connection Security

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

1. Network allowlist
2. TLS
3. Authentication
4. Authorization
5. Database access

Fix the layer the error names. Do not disable them all to “just connect.”

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/56-layered-connection-security.svg" alt="Allowlist, TLS, authentication, authorization, database access" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Safe Credential Practices

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Dedicated database users
- Strong unique passwords
- No secrets in source or screenshots
- Environment variables or a secret store
- Restrict network access
- Encrypt remote connections
- Least-privilege roles
- Rotate exposed credentials

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/55-credential-antipattern-vs-secure.svg" alt="Hard-coded password versus secret store" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Common Installation Problems

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Unsupported OS or missing requirements
- Insufficient permissions
- Wrong package or repository
- Port already in use
- Invalid data-directory path or permissions
- Invalid config syntax
- Service not registered
- Insufficient disk space

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/62-startup-failure-diagnosis.svg" alt="Start request through config, permissions, port conflict, to the server log" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Common Connection Problems

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

| Symptom | Typical cause |
|---------|----------------|
| Connection refused | Stopped server or wrong port |
| Timeout | Firewall, routing, allowlist |
| Auth failed | User, password, or auth DB |
| Host not found | Hostname or DNS |
| TLS error | Certificate / encryption mismatch |
| Unauthorized | Role too weak |

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/64-common-error-decision-tree.svg" alt="Error types branching to corrective actions" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Troubleshooting Workflow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Read the error → URI → server up? → host/port → network → credentials → logs → simplest client.

**Key message:** Change **one** variable, then retest.

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/57-troubleshooting-workflow.svg" alt="Error, service, host/port, network, auth, logs, retest" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 2.4 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 2.4`](../slide-exercises/module-02/exercise-2.4-diagnose-connection-failures.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Diagnose ECONNREFUSED and authentication failure**
- **Do:** For `ECONNREFUSED` and authentication failure, fill likely cause, first check, relevant log or setting, corrective action, and verification command.
- **Expected:** Refused connection points at a stopped server or wrong port. Authentication failure points at user, password, or authentication database — not at DNS.

**Step 2 — Diagnose timeout and DNS failure**
- **Do:** Repeat for server-selection timeout and DNS lookup failure.
- **Expected:** Timeout points at firewall, routing, or network allowlist. DNS failure points at hostname or DNS, not at a missing role.

**Step 3 — Diagnose unauthorized command and invalid URI**
- **Do:** Repeat for unauthorized operation and invalid connection-string format.
- **Expected:** Unauthorized means the user authenticated but lacks the role. Invalid URI means syntax, unencoded special characters, or the wrong scheme.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

## Exercise 2.4 — Steps 3–4

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 2.4`](../slide-exercises/module-02/exercise-2.4-diagnose-connection-failures.md)
**Step 3 — Diagnose unauthorized command and invalid URI**
- **Do:** Repeat for unauthorized operation and invalid connection-string format.
- **Expected:** Unauthorized = logged in, role too weak. Bad URI = syntax or encoding.

**Step 4 — Compare with the instructor solution**
- **Do:** Share one case. Change one variable, then ping.
- **Expected:** A consistent diagnostic sequence, not three simultaneous guesses.

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

Before Module 3:

- Installed or provisioned
- Server running · clients available
- URI stored **securely**
- Auth works · network allowed
- Ping `ok: 1`
- Insert and retrieve succeed

## Exercise 2.3 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 2.3`](../slide-exercises/module-02/exercise-2.3-environment-readiness-checklist.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Record environment details**
- **Do:** Write down (without secrets) whether you are using local, container, managed cloud, or an instructor-provided instance. Note hostname or cluster name and port if it is not the default `27017`.
- **Expected:** You can state your deployment path and how you reach the server, with no password on the page.

**Step 2 — Confirm clients and connection information**
- **Do:** Check that `mongosh` is available (`mongosh --version`). If Compass is required, confirm it launches. Confirm you have a connection string stored securely (password manager, instructor handout, or environment variable) —
- **Expected:** Shell version prints. Compass opens if required. You know where the URI lives without displaying the password.

**Step 3 — Confirm ping, write, and read**
- **Do:** In `mongosh`, run `db.runCommand({ ping: 1 })`. Then confirm you can insert and retrieve a document in `training_store` (Exercise 2.5 covers the commands). Tick ping, insert, and read only if you saw the results.
- **Expected:** Ping contains `ok: 1`. A test document can be inserted and found. You did not tick a box you did not prove.

# Module Summary

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- MongoDB may run locally, in a container, on a server, or as a managed service
- `mongod` is the server; `mongosh` and Compass are clients
- Connection strings describe how clients reach MongoDB
- Ping verifies connectivity; write-and-read verifies usable access
- Protect credentials and network access

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-02/12-client-connection-options.svg" alt="Three clients converging on one MongoDB deployment" width="720">

</div>
</div>

9. Common cause of authentication failed?
10. Why not embed credentials in source code?

# Data Modeling with MongoDB

Effective MongoDB schemas are designed around how an application reads, writes, and changes data

<!-- _class: content -->

# Module Learning Objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to:

- Interpret MongoDB document structures
- Select appropriate BSON types
- Identify common access patterns
- Model relationships with embedding or references
- Control document and array growth
- Apply schema-validation rules
- Design the course sample application database

# Why Data Modeling Matters

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Efficient retrieval
- Safer related updates
- Predictable document shape
- Indexes that match queries
- **Key message:** MongoDB removes rigid tables, not the need for design

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/000-why-data-modeling-matters.svg" alt="Good model outcomes versus poor model problems" width="720">

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- A document holds fields, nested documents, and arrays
- This course uses **training_store**

</div>

# Databases, Collections, and Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Database:** logical container
- **Collection:** related documents
- **Document:** field-value pairs
- **Field:** a named element inside a document

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/002-database-collection-document.svg" alt="Database to collection to document to field" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# A Product Document

```javascript
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  sku: "P1001",
  name: "Wireless Keyboard",
  price: 49.99
}
```

Collection: `products` in database `training_store`.

`sku` is a **business** identifier. `_id` is the **document** identifier.

# Anatomy — labeled example

```javascript
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  name: "Wireless Keyboard",
  price: Decimal128("49.99"),
  active: true,
  tags: ["wireless", "accessories"],
  specifications: {
    connection: "Bluetooth",
    batteryLifeMonths: 12
  },
  createdAt: ISODate("2026-09-20T10:00:00Z")
}
```

# Understanding BSON Data Types

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Type choice affects precision, sorting, comparison, and storage
- Money → **Decimal128**, not Double
- Timestamps → **Date**, not display strings

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/004-bson-data-type-map.svg" alt="BSON types and typical uses" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# ObjectId and the `_id` Field

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Every document needs a unique `_id`
- MongoDB often generates an ObjectId
- You may supply a business key instead
- Indexed automatically and treated as immutable

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/005-id-field-and-objectid.svg" alt="Default ObjectId versus application-defined _id" width="720">

# Nested Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Related data as an embedded object
- Fits when the child belongs to the parent
- Retrieved with the parent
- Stays bounded

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Label identifier, scalars, and the nested name**
- **Do:** On the sample document, mark `_id`, every scalar field (`customerNumber`, `email`), and the embedded `name` document. Write one sentence: what does `_id` guarantee inside a collection?
- **Expected:** `_id` is the unique identifier. `customerNumber` and `email` are scalars. `name` is an embedded document with `first` and `last`.

**Step 2 — Label array, Boolean, date, and required fields**
- **Do:** Mark `tags` as an array, `active` as a Boolean, and `createdAt` as a Date. Then list candidate **required** fields for every customer document in this collection.
- **Expected:** You named `tags`, `active`, and `createdAt` correctly. Required-field candidates typically include `_id` (always), `customerNumber`, `name`, `email` or contact,

# Relational Modeling vs Document Modeling

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Relational: normalize first, join later
- Document: start with access patterns
- Store related data together when it is used together

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/011-relational-vs-document-model.svg" alt="Relational approach compared with document approach" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Tables to Documents Transformation

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Fold `order_items` and `addresses` into the order
- Keep `products` and `customers` as collections
- Reviews stay independent

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

</div>
</div>

# Join-Based Retrieval vs Document Retrieval

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Relational: several joins to paint one screen
- Document: `find` the order number
- The document **is** the business object

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/013-join-vs-document-retrieval.svg" alt="Multiple joins compared with one document read" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Relational Normalization vs MongoDB Aggregates

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Normalization divides by entity
- Document modeling groups by operation
- Split only what must live apart

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/014-normalization-vs-aggregates.svg" alt="Entity tables compared with an order aggregate" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Avoid the Collection-per-Table Anti-Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Tiny collections keep the joins
- Redesign around aggregates
- `training_store` uses four collections, not twelve tables

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/015-collection-per-table-antipattern.svg" alt="Table copies versus a redesigned document model" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Read and Write Access Patterns

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Reads: locate, return, latency
- Writes: which fields, how often, concurrency
- One fast read can make writes harder

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/017-read-and-write-access-patterns.svg" alt="Read considerations versus write considerations" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Embedding speeds the hot read
- Writes may touch a larger document
- Accept that cost on purpose

</div>

# Demo 3.2 — Compare Relational and Document Models

**Duration:** 15 minutes

Show five tables: `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, `addresses`.

Then one **order document**: customer reference, embedded items, shipping snapshot, status, total.

**Outcome:** modeling focuses on aggregates and access patterns, not on 1:1 table copies.

# Relationship Types

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- One-to-one, one-to-few, one-to-many
- One-to-squillions, many-to-many
- Size, growth, ownership, and access direction decide the shape

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/023-mongodb-relationship-types.svg" alt="Cardinality spectrum from 1:1 to many-to-many" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 3 on the slide: Size, growth, ownership, and access direction decide the shape.

The figure on this slide is titled: Cardinality spectrum from 1:1 to many-to-many.
-->

<!-- _class: split -->

# One-to-One Relationships

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Embed when the child exists only as part of the parent
- Reference when the child has its own lifecycle

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/024-one-to-one-relationship.svg" alt="Embedded contact versus referenced profile" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Embed when the child exists only as part of the parent.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Reference when the child has its own lifecycle.

The figure on this slide is titled: Embedded contact versus referenced profile.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# One-to-Few Relationships

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- A handful of children, bounded
- Customer addresses, product images
- Embed as an array of documents

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/025-one-to-few-relationship.svg" alt="Customer with a bounded addresses array" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The figure on this slide is titled: Customer with a bounded addresses array.
-->

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# One-to-Many Relationships

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **One-to-few:** addresses, images, order items — embed
- **One-to-many / unbounded:** orders, reviews, transactions — reference

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/026-one-to-many-relationship.svg" alt="One-to-few embed versus one-to-many reference" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# One-to-Squillions Relationships

- Own collection, paginated

- Choice depends on navigation and update cost

<!-- _class: split -->

# Relationship Cardinality Decision Flow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- How many — and will it grow?
- One or few and bounded → embed
- Many or unbounded → reference

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/029-relationship-cardinality-decision.svg" alt="Cardinality leading to embed or reference" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: One or few and bounded → embed.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Many or unbounded → reference.

The figure on this slide is titled: Cardinality leading to embed or reference.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Relationship Ownership

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Owned by the parent → embed candidate
- Independently managed → reference
- Cardinality without ownership is incomplete

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/030-relationship-ownership.svg" alt="Owned child data versus independently managed related data" width="720">

</div>
</div>

This slide includes a diagram — Relationship Ownership.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Owned by the parent → embed candidate.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Independently managed → reference.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Cardinality without ownership is incomplete.

The figure on this slide is titled: Owned child data versus independently managed related data.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Embedding Related Data

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- One operation retrieves the aggregate
- Single-document updates are atomic
- Risks: duplication, growth, bulk updates

# Maintaining Duplicated Data

Ask: **must the copy always match the source?**

Possible strategies:

- Treat it as a historical snapshot
- Update in the application
- Update asynchronously
- Rebuild periodically
- Allow eventual consistency
- Copy only stable fields

# Exercise 3.3 — Embed or Reference?

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- 15 minutes · eight relationships
- Justify with ownership, cardinality, growth
- Only office address is a true ‘it depends’

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 3.3`](../slide-exercises/module-03/exercise-3.3-embed-or-reference.md)

## Exercise 3.4 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 3.4`](../slide-exercises/module-03/exercise-3.4-model-a-product-catalog.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Design the shared core**
- **Do:** List the common field names and BSON types (`sku` string, `price` Decimal128, `active` Boolean, `createdAt` Date). Decide whether category-specific fields live at the top level or under `attributes`.
- **Expected:** One core field list used by all three products. You did not invent `productPrice` on one document and `price` on another.

**Step 2 — Write three documents**
- **Do:** Draft one laptop, one shoe, and one book in the same `products` collection. Keep the core identical. Put type-specific data in `attributes` (or an equivalent nested object).
- **Expected:** Three documents that a later `find({ category: "LAPTOP" })` and `find({ "attributes.isbn": ... })` could use. Category-specific fields do not appear as required

## Exercise 3.5 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 3.5`](../slide-exercises/module-03/exercise-3.5-model-an-order-document.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Decide embed versus reference**
- **Do:** Write four decisions: line items, purchase-time price, shipping address, customer. Mark which of those are **historical snapshots**.
- **Expected:** Items, prices, and shipping address are embedded snapshots. Customer is a reference (`customerId`). Current product catalog is not copied in full.

**Step 2 — Write the document and required fields**
- **Do:** Draft one order document including `orderNumber`, `customerId`, `items[]` (sku, name, quantity, unitPrice), `shippingAddress`, statuses, monetary totals as Decimal128, and `createdAt`. List required fields.
- **Expected:** A complete order JSON-like object plus a short justification: one read by order number, customer orders via `customerId`, prices never silently follow the catal

# Unbounded Arrays

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `allReviews: [ /* millions */ ]` will hurt
- Large docs, expensive updates, 16 MiB risk
- Put high-cardinality children in their own collection

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/048-unbounded-array-antipattern.svg" alt="Danger of unbounded reviews array and the better design" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Bounded vs Unbounded Arrays

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Addresses: you can name a max
- All reviews: you cannot
- If you cannot name a max, do not embed

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/047-bounded-vs-unbounded-arrays.svg" alt="Small address array compared with growing reviews" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# JSON Schema — product example

```javascript
db.createCollection("products", {
  validator: {
    $jsonSchema: {
      bsonType: "object",
      required: ["sku", "name", "price"],
      properties: {
        sku: { bsonType: "string" },
        name: { bsonType: "string" },
        price: { bsonType: "decimal", minimum: 0 }
      }
    }
  }
})
```

## Exercise 3.6 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 3.6`](../slide-exercises/module-03/exercise-3.6-correct-schema-anti-patterns.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Name the problems**
- **Do:** List every issue you can see: types, growth, naming, identifier strategy.
- **Expected:** Price stored as a string; Boolean stored as text; unbounded `allReviews` array; nonstandard date string; identifier is `productId` rather than `_id` or `sku` wi

**Step 2 — Rewrite the document**
- **Do:** Produce a corrected document. Move reviews out (reference). Use Decimal128, Boolean, Date, and a clear `_id`/`sku` convention.
- **Expected:** Something like `sku`/`_id`, `price: Decimal128("49.99")`, `active: true`, `createdAt: ISODate(...)`, and **no** `allReviews` array.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

## Exercise 3.8 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 3.8`](../slide-exercises/module-03/exercise-3.8-design-collection-validation.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — List required fields and bsonTypes**
- **Do:** Write the `required` array and a `properties` map with `bsonType` for each field. Put `minimum: 0` on `price`.
- **Expected:** Six required names. `price` is `decimal` (not `double` or `string`). `active` is `bool`. `createdAt` is `date`.

**Step 2 — Assemble `$jsonSchema`**
- **Do:** Wrap the design in: javascript { $jsonSchema: { bsonType: "object", required: [ /* ... */ ], properties: { /* ... */ } } }  Note `validationAction` / `validationLevel` if you know them. You will apply a similar val
- **Expected:** A complete validator object you could pass to `db.createCollection`. Extra optional fields are still allowed.

<!-- _class: split -->

# Common MongoDB Schema Patterns

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Reusable approaches, not mandatory templates
- Attribute, Bucket, Subset, Extended reference
- Computed, Outlier, Polymorphic

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/078-schema-pattern-overview.svg" alt="Seven named MongoDB schema patterns" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Common MongoDB Schema Patterns.

The slide title is: Common MongoDB Schema Patterns.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Reusable approaches, not mandatory templates.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Attribute, Bucket, Subset, Extended reference.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Computed, Outlier, Polymorphic.

The figure on this slide is titled: Seven named MongoDB schema patterns.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Attribute Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Many similar optional attributes
- `attributes: [ { name, value } ]`
- Easier to index than fifty sparse fields

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/079-attribute-pattern.svg" alt="Named fields versus name-value attribute array" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Attribute Pattern.

The slide title is: Attribute Pattern.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Many similar optional attributes.

Bullet 2 on the slide: attributes: [ { name, value } ].

Bullet 3 on the slide: Easier to index than fifty sparse fields.

The figure on this slide is titled: Named fields versus name-value attribute array.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Bucket Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Group measurements into a bounded document
- Sensor hour, metrics, events
- Fewer documents, controlled growth

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/080-bucket-pattern.svg" alt="Hour bucket containing a bounded readings array" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Bucket Pattern.

The slide title is: Bucket Pattern.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Group measurements into a bounded document.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Sensor hour, metrics, events.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Fewer documents, controlled growth.

The figure on this slide is titled: Hour bucket containing a bounded readings array.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Subset Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Keep the hot subset on the parent
- Full set lives elsewhere
- Example: three recent reviews plus average rating

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/081-subset-pattern.svg" alt="Product subset versus full reviews collection" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Subset Pattern.

The slide title is: Subset Pattern.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Keep the hot subset on the parent.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Full set lives elsewhere.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Example: three recent reviews plus average rating.

The figure on this slide is titled: Product subset versus full reviews collection.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Extended Reference Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Copy frequently displayed fields onto the reference
- Order stores customer name and tier
- Tradeoff: those copies may need sync

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/082-extended-reference-pattern.svg" alt="Order carrying a small customer summary" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Extended Reference Pattern.

The slide title is: Extended Reference Pattern.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Copy frequently displayed fields onto the reference.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Order stores customer name and tier.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Tradeoff: those copies may need sync.

The figure on this slide is titled: Order carrying a small customer summary.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Computed Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Store the result instead of recomputing on every read
- Average rating, order total, lifetime value
- Must update when the source changes

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/083-computed-pattern.svg" alt="Stored rating summary on a product" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Computed Pattern.

The slide title is: Computed Pattern.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Store the result instead of recomputing on every read.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Average rating, order total, lifetime value.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Must update when the source changes.

The figure on this slide is titled: Stored rating summary on a product.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Outlier Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Most documents follow the normal design
- Rare extremes get a different store
- Do not distort the schema for one viral product

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/084-outlier-pattern.svg" alt="Typical products versus viral products" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Outlier Pattern.

The slide title is: Outlier Pattern.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Most documents follow the normal design.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Rare extremes get a different store.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Do not distort the schema for one viral product.

The figure on this slide is titled: Typical products versus viral products.
-->

---































<!-- _class: split -->

# Polymorphic Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Different types share one collection and a core
- A `type` or `category` field distinguishes them
- Same workflows, varied attributes

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/085-polymorphic-pattern.svg" alt="BOOK and LAPTOP documents in one collection" width="720">

</div>
</div>

This slide includes a diagram — Polymorphic Pattern.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Different types share one collection and a core.

Bullet 2 on the slide: A type or category field distinguishes them.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Same workflows, varied attributes.

The figure on this slide is titled: BOOK and LAPTOP documents in one collection.
-->

---

# Choosing an Appropriate Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Start from the requirement, then pick a pattern
- You may combine patterns in one model

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/086-schema-pattern-selection-matrix.svg" alt="Requirements mapped to schema patterns" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Combining Schema Patterns

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Patterns compose on one document
- Catalog: polymorphic + attribute + computed + subset
- Outlier handles the viral SKU

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-03/087-combining-schema-patterns.svg" alt="Product using attribute, subset, computed, and outlier together" width="720">

</div>
</div>

```javascript
db.products.find({ "attributes.memoryGB": 16 })
db.products.find({ tags: "technology" })
db.customers.find({ "addresses.city": "Toronto" })
db.orders.find({ "items.sku": "L100" })
```

## Exercise 3.9 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 3.9`](../slide-exercises/module-03/exercise-3.9-support-ticket-challenge.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Access patterns and collections**
- **Do:** List the main access patterns. Name the collections. Mark what is embedded vs referenced, and what could grow without bound.
- **Expected:** Collections such as `tickets`, `customers`, `agents`, `comments` and/or `audit_events`. Recent comments and tags are bounded on the ticket. Full comment and aud

**Step 2 — Sample document, validation, and indexes**
- **Do:** Draft one ticket document with BSON types. List required fields for validation. Explain how complete audit history is stored. Name likely future indexes (do **not** create them yet).
- **Expected:** A ticket with `ticketNumber`, `customerId`, `assignee`, `status`, `priority`, `tags`, `recentComments[]`, timestamps. Validation requires those keys. Audit even

# Exit Ticket

1. Database vs collection vs document?
2. Why is `_id` important?
3. JSON vs BSON?
4. What is an access pattern?
5. When to embed? When to reference?
6. Why are unbounded arrays dangerous?
7. Why duplicate product info on an order?
8. Purpose of collection validation?
9. How can a schema evolve safely?
10. Pattern for time-series? For calculated values?

Participants can:

- Design a valid BSON document and choose types
- Identify access patterns and relationship types
- Justify embedding and referencing
- Recognize unbounded arrays
- Apply at least one named schema pattern
- Create and populate related collections
- Query embedded fields and arrays
- Create basic collection validation

# Module Learning Objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to:

- Write accurate query filters
- Retrieve required fields with projections
- Work with nested values and arrays
- Insert valid documents and verify writes
- Update scalar, nested, and array fields
- Replace or upsert documents
- Delete test records safely
- Interpret write-operation results

# MongoDB CRUD Operations

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Create** `insertOne()` · `insertMany()`
- **Read** `findOne()` · `find()`
- **Update** `updateOne()` · `updateMany()`
- **Replace** `replaceOne()`
- **Delete** `deleteOne()` · `deleteMany()`
- Always verify the result

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/001-crud-operations-overview.svg" alt="CRUD operations and common methods" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# CRUD Flow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Start from a business requirement
- Name the collection and the filter
- Choose the CRUD method
- Read matchedCount / insertedId / deletedCount
- Query again to confirm

</div>

# MongoDB Query Anatomy

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `db` — current database
- `products` — collection
- `find()` — operation
- First document — **filter**
- Second document — **projection**
- General: `db.collection.method(filter, options)`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/002-query-anatomy.svg" alt="Anatomy of a find call" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Understanding Query Filters

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `{}` matches **every** document
- `{ category: "LAPTOP" }` is equality
- Two fields → **implicit AND**
- Empty filters are legal on `find`
- Empty filters are disastrous on `deleteMany`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/008-empty-vs-targeted-filter.svg" alt="Empty filter versus a targeted category filter" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--

# `findOne()` vs `find()`

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `findOne()` returns one document or `null`
- `find()` returns a **cursor** of 0..n documents
- Use `findOne` when one result is expected
- Use `find` when you may have many — then sort/limit

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/007-findone-vs-find.svg" alt="findOne returns one document; find returns a cursor" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Retrieving All Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `db.products.find({})` matches every document
- `mongosh` prints from the cursor
- Fine on the training catalog
- On large collections: filter, project, and limit
- Empty `find` is a scan, not a dump strategy

</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Equality Filters

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `{ active: true }` is one-field equality
- `{ category: "BOOK", active: true }` is implicit AND
- Field names are case-sensitive
- String values are case-sensitive
- `{ Category: "laptop" }` matches nothing here

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/009-equality-filter.svg" alt="Product documents passing a category equality filter" width="720">

</div>
</div>

- Always quote dotted field paths

# Comparison Operators

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$eq` `$ne` equal / not equal
- `$gt` `$gte` greater / or equal
- `$lt` `$lte` less / or equal
- Put operators **inside** the field
- Money: `Decimal128("50.00")`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

</div>

# The `$in` and `$nin` Operators

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$in` — field matches **any** listed value
- `category: { $in: ["BOOK", "ACCESSORY"] }`
- `$nin` — field matches **none** of the list
- `$in` is cleaner than `$or` on one field
- One accepted value vs several accepted values

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/017-in-operator.svg" alt="One field matching any value from a permitted list" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Logical Operators

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$and` — all expressions match
- `$or` — at least one matches
- `$nor` — none may match
- `$not` — negate a field-level condition
- Prefer implicit AND when fields differ

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/021-logical-operators-overview.svg" alt="Logical operator meanings" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Combining Query Conditions

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Implicit AND: two fields in one document
- Explicit `$and`: same field, two tests
- Nest `$or` inside an AND document
- Read the filter out loud as English

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/026-combined-logical-query.svg" alt="Implicit AND, explicit AND, nested OR" width="720">

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# The `$not` and `$nor` Operators

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$not` negates a **field-level** condition
- `$nor` rejects documents matching **any** listed condition
- Negation can also match **missing** fields
- Preview `$not` / `$nor` before using them in writes
- Prefer `$ne` or `$nin` when the intent is simpler

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/024-nor-operator.svg" alt="Documents rejected if they match any prohibited condition" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Field Existence, BSON Type, Null

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$exists: true/false` — field present?
- `$type: "decimal"` vs `"string"`
- `{ phone: null }` matches null **or missing**
- `$type: "null"` — explicitly null
- `$exists: false` — field absent

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/030-null-vs-missing.svg" alt="Null query versus type null versus missing field" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Regular-Expression Queries

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Prefix: `{ $regex: "^Mongo", $options: "i" }`
- Regex can be expensive
- Anchored (`^`) is more index-friendly
- Unanchored search scans the field
- Atlas Search is better for real full-text

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/035-prefix-search.svg" alt="Anchored prefix search matching names that start with Mongo" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 4.1 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.1`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.1-read-basic-documents.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Retrieve all products**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({})
- **Expected:** A cursor of product documents prints. This is unbounded — acceptable on the training set only.

**Step 2 — Find one product by SKU**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.findOne({ sku: "L100" })
- **Expected:** One laptop document is returned. `findOne()` returns a document or `null`, not a cursor.

**Step 3 — Find active products**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ active: true })
- **Expected:** Inactive items such as `L190` are excluded. Field names and booleans are case-sensitive.

## Exercise 4.2 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.2`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.2-build-comparison-filters.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Products priced above 100**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ price: { $gt: Decimal128("100.00") } })
- **Expected:** Laptops and `S200` appear. `XBAD` does not — its price is a string, not Decimal128.

**Step 2 — Products priced between 50 and 500**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ price: { $gte: Decimal128("50.00"), $lte: Decimal128("500.00") } })
- **Expected:** Includes `S200`, `S210`, `A400`, and similar mid-range items. Both bounds are inclusive.

**Step 3 — Orders with totals above 1,000**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.orders.find({ total: { $gt: Decimal128("1000.00") } })
- **Expected:** `O5001` and `O6401` match (both contain L100 and have totals above 1,000). Paid high-value orders such as `O6101` also match.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

## Exercise 4.3 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.3`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.3-combine-logical-conditions.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Active laptops or books**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ active: true, $or: [ { category: "LAPTOP" }, { category: "BOOK" } ] })
- **Expected:** Active laptops and books match. Inactive `L190` is excluded by `active: true`.

**Step 2 — Active products under 100**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ active: true, price: { $lt: Decimal128("100.00") } })
- **Expected:** Implicit AND. Accessories and cheaper books match. `XBAD` does not, because of BSON type.

**Step 3 — Pending or processing orders**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.orders.find({ $or: [ { paymentStatus: "PENDING" }, { fulfillmentStatus: "PROCESSING" } ] })
- **Expected:** `O5001` and `O6499` are PENDING payment; `O6401` is PROCESSING. Prefer `$in` when alternatives share **one** field.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

## Exercise 4.3 — Steps 3–4

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 3 — Pending or processing orders**
- **Do:** Run: ` db.orders.find({ $or: [ { paymentStatus: "PENDING" }, { fulfillmentStatus: "PROCESSING" } ] }) `
- **Expected:** `O5001` and `O6499` are PENDING payment; `O6401` is PROCESSING. Prefer `$in` when alternatives share **one** field.

**Step 4 — Neither discontinued nor inactive**
- **Do:** Run: ` db.products.find({ $nor: [ { tags: "discontinued" }, { active: false } ] }) `
- **Expected:** Documents that are inactive **or** tagged `discontinued` are excluded. `L190` is both.

**Step 1 — Products with a discount field**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ discountPrice: { $exists: true } })
- **Expected:** `P1001` and `B310` match. Presence of the field is enough — the value may still be inspected later.

**Step 2 — Products without a discount field**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ discountPrice: { $exists: false } })
- **Expected:** Most catalog items match, including laptops that never had a discount field.

**Step 3 — Customers with a null phone**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.customers.find({ "contact.phone": { $type: "null" } })
- **Expected:** `C204` matches. `{ phone: null }` on a dotted path is easy to get wrong — query `{ "contact.phone": { $type: "null" } }`.

# Querying Arrays

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `tags: "technology"` — **contains** that element
- Does **not** require matching the whole array
- Exact array: values **and** order **and** length
- `$all` — contains all values, any order
- `$size` — exact length only, not a range

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/038-array-query-fundamentals.svg" alt="Array containment versus exact match versus all versus size" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: Does not require matching the whole array.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Exact array: values and order and length.

Bullet 4 on the slide: $all — contains all values, any order.

Bullet 5 on the slide: $size — exact length only, not a range.

The figure on this slide is titled: Array containment versus exact match versus all versus size.

# Exact Array Matching vs `$all` vs `$size`

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Exact match: values **and** order **and** length
- `$all` — contains all values, any order, extras allowed
- `$size` — exact element count only
- L100 has three tags — exact two-element match fails
- `$size` cannot express “at least two”

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/041-all-operator.svg" alt="Array required to contain all specified values regardless of order" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# The `$elemMatch` Operator

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Use when **two conditions** must hit the **same** array element
- Without it, `items.sku` and `items.quantity` can match **different** lines
- Teaching trap: **O5001** has L100 qty 1 and A200 qty 2
- Only **O6401** has L100 qty 2

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/045-why-elemmatch.svg" alt="elemMatch versus matching different array elements" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Querying Arrays of Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `"items.sku": "L100"` — any line item with that SKU
- `$elemMatch` when two conditions must hit **one** element
- O5001 has L100 qty 1 and A410 qty 2 — the trap
- Only O6401 has L100 qty 2 on the **same** line
- Dot notation is enough for “contains this product”

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/044-querying-field-inside-array.svg" alt="Dot notation navigating from items to sku" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Demo 4.3 — Query Nested Documents and Arrays

**Duration:** 15 minutes

```javascript
db.products.find({ "attributes.memoryGB": { $gte: 16 } })
db.customers.find({ "addresses.city": "Toronto" })
db.orders.find({
  items: { $elemMatch: { sku: "L100", quantity: { $gte: 1 } } }
})
```

Then contrast the **without** `$elemMatch` form on O5001.

**Step 3 — Exactly two tags**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ tags: { $size: 2 } })
- **Expected:** Most catalog products have exactly two tags. `$size` cannot express “at least two”.

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.6`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.6-query-arrays-of-documents.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Orders containing SKU L100**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.orders.find({ "items.sku": "L100" })
- **Expected:** `O5001`, `O6101`, and `O6401` match.

**Step 2 — Orders with any item quantity ≥ 2**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.orders.find({ "items.quantity": { $gte: 2 } })
- **Expected:** `O5001` (A410 qty 2) and `O6401` (L100 qty 2). Other orders may also match.

**Step 3 — Same item is L100 and qty ≥ 2**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.orders.find({ items: { $elemMatch: { sku: "L100", quantity: { $gte: 2 } } } })
- **Expected:** Only `O6401`. `O5001` has L100 qty 1 **and** a different item (A410) qty 2 — that is the trap.

# Projection Fundamentals

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Projection controls **which fields** return
- Inclusion: `{ name: 1, price: 1 }`
- Exclusion: `{ attributes: 0, tags: 0 }`
- Do **not** mix inclusion and exclusion
- Exception: `_id` may be excluded from an inclusion

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/048-filter-vs-projection.svg" alt="Inclusion versus exclusion projections" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 3 on the slide: Exclusion: { attributes: 0, tags: 0 }.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Do not mix inclusion and exclusion.

Bullet 5 on the slide: Exception: _id may be excluded from an inclusion.

The figure on this slide is titled: Inclusion versus exclusion projections.

# Inclusion, Exclusion, Nested, and Array Projection

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Inclusion: `{ name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 }`
- Nested: `{ "name.first": 1, "contact.email": 1 }`
- Array `$elemMatch` in projection returns **one** matching element
- `$slice` returns first or most recent elements
- Projection `$elemMatch` is not the same as the filter form

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/049-inclusion-projection.svg" alt="Complete document reduced to selected fields" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Cursor Fundamentals

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `find()` returns a cursor, not an array
- Chain `.sort()` `.limit()` `.skip()`
- Iterate; do not always `.toArray()` a huge result
- Conceptual order: filter → project → sort → limit

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/057-filter-sort-limit.svg" alt="find then sort then skip/limit then iterate" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split fit-md -->

# Sorting, Limiting, Skipping, Pagination

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `.sort({ category: 1, price: -1, _id: 1 })` — tiebreaker
- `.limit(5)` then `.skip(5).limit(5)` for page 2
- `skip()` is fine for shallow pages
- Deep skip is expensive — range on last-seen value instead
- Always sort if you paginate

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/062-skip-limit-pagination.svg" alt="Sorted results divided into pages using offset and page size" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Counting and Distinct Values

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `countDocuments(filter)` — accurate filtered count
- `estimatedDocumentCount()` — fast estimate
- `distinct("category")` — unique values
- Prefer `countDocuments` over legacy `count()`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/065-count-operations.svg" alt="countDocuments versus estimated versus distinct" width="720">

</div>
</div>

```javascript
db.products
  .find({ active: true }, { name: 1, category: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 })
  .sort({ price: -1 })
  .limit(5)
```

## Exercise 4.8 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.8`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.8-sort-and-paginate.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Sort products by price ascending**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({}, { name: 1, price: 1 }).sort({ price: 1, _id: 1 })
- **Expected:** Cheapest Decimal128 prices first. `XBAD` may sort oddly because its price is a string — mention that.

**Step 2 — Sort by category then price descending**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({}, { category: 1, name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 }) .sort({ category: 1, price: -1 })
- **Expected:** Within each category the highest price prints first.

**Step 3 — Five most expensive active products**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.find({ active: true }, { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 }) .sort({ price: -1, _id: 1 }) .limit(5)
- **Expected:** Expect `L110`, `L100`, then `L190` if active were included — on active-only, `L110` then `L100` then `A500`.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

## Exercise 4.8 — Steps 3–4

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 3 — Five most expensive active products**
- **Do:** Run: ` db.products.find({ active: true }, { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 }) .sort({ price: -1, _id: 1 }) .limit(5) `
- **Expected:** Expect `L110`, `L100`, then `L190` if active were included — on active-only, `L110` then `L100` then `A500`.

**Step 4 — Page 1 and page 2 (five per page)**
- **Do:** Run both: ` db.products.find({ active: true }).sort({ _id: 1 }).skip(0).limit(5) db.products.find({ active: true }).sort({ _id: 1 }).skip(5).limit(5) `
- **Expected:** Two disjoint pages. The sort key is required for stable pagination.

# Inserting Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `insertOne(document)`
- `insertMany([ ... ])`
- Result: `acknowledged`, `insertedId(s)`
- Then `findOne` by SKU — always
- Keep money as Decimal128, dates as Date

</div>

# Insert One and Many

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `insertOne` — one document, one `insertedId`
- `insertMany` — one request, several documents
- Keep money as Decimal128 and dates as Date
- Reserved lab SKUs: `A620`, `A610`–`A612`, `A700`, `A800`, `TEMP-*`
- Always `findOne` by SKU after insert

</div>

- **Expected:** `insertedIds` contains three keys. Inspect `insertedCount` / `insertedIds`.

- **Expected:** One customer with nested `name`, `contact`, and `addresses`.

# Updating Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `updateOne` — first match only
- `updateMany` — every match; **preview first**
- `$set` changes listed fields only
- `$unset` removes a field
- `$inc` `$mul` `$min` `$max` `$rename`

</div>

# `$set`, `$unset`, Numeric Operators, `$rename`

```javascript
{ $set: { featured: true, "attributes.warrantyYears": 2 } }
{ $unset: { temporaryNote: "" } }
{ $inc: { stockQuantity: 5 } }
{ $mul: { price: 1.05 } }   // beware Decimal128 vs double
{ $min: { lowestPrice: Decimal128("45.00") } }
{ $rename: { productName: "name" } }
```

Use consistent numeric types. Prefer `$inc` on integers. Be careful multiplying money.

# Updating Nested Fields

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$set: { "contact.email": "new@..." }` — targeted
- `$set: { contact: { email: ... } }` — **replaces** the object
- Sibling fields such as `phone` disappear
- Dot notation is the default safe habit

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/084-targeted-vs-object-replacement.svg" alt="Targeted nested set versus replacing the whole object" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: $set: { "contact.email": "new@..." } — targeted.

Bullet 2 on the slide: $set: { contact: { email: ... } } — replaces the object.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Sibling fields such as phone disappear.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Dot notation is the default safe habit.

The figure on this slide is titled: Targeted nested set versus replacing the whole object.
