## Exercise 4.10 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.10`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.10-update-product-data.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Preview then change a price**
- **Do:** Run the filter first, then: javascript db.products.find({ sku: "A620" }) db.products.updateOne( { sku: "A620" }, { $set: { price: Decimal128("64.99"), updatedAt: new Date() } } )
- **Expected:** `matchedCount: 1`, `modifiedCount: 1` if the price changed. If A620 is missing, complete Exercise 4.9 first.

**Step 2 — Add a nested warranty field**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.updateOne( { sku: "L100" }, { $set: { "attributes.warrantyYears": 2 } } )
- **Expected:** `attributes` still contains `memoryGB`. The warranty field is added beside it.

**Step 3 — Increase inventory**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.updateOne({ sku: "L100" }, { $inc: { stockQuantity: 5 } })
- **Expected:** `stockQuantity` increases by 5 (from 8 to 13 on a fresh load).

# Array Update Operators

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$push` — add; **may duplicate**
- `$addToSet` — add if absent
- `$pull` / `$pullAll` — remove by match / values
- `$pop` — first (`-1`) or last (`1`)
- Modifiers: `$each` `$position` `$sort` `$slice`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/089-array-update-operators.svg" alt="Array update operators" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: $addToSet — add if absent.

Bullet 3 on the slide: $pull / $pullAll — remove by match / values.

Bullet 4 on the slide: $pop — first (-1) or last (1).

Bullet 5 on the slide: Modifiers: $each $position $sort $slice.

The figure on this slide is titled: Array update operators.

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$each` — several values
- `$position` — insert index
- `$sort` — order the array
- `$slice` — bound length (recent events)

# Positional Array Updates

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `items.$` — first **matched** element (query must identify it)
- `items.$[]` — **all** elements
- `items.$[item]` — filtered elements
- Requires `arrayFilters` for the identifier

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

## Exercise 4.11 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.11`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.11-modify-arrays.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Push a tag (may duplicate)**
- **Do:** Run twice: javascript db.products.updateOne({ sku: "A620" }, { $push: { tags: "featured" } })
- **Expected:** The second run adds a second `featured` if you used `$push` both times. That is the teaching point.

**Step 2 — Add a tag without duplicates**
- **Do:** Run twice: javascript db.products.updateOne({ sku: "A620" }, { $addToSet: { tags: "office" } })
- **Expected:** Second run: `matchedCount: 1`, `modifiedCount: 0` if `office` is already present.

**Step 3 — Add several tags**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.updateOne( { sku: "A620" }, { $addToSet: { tags: { $each: ["portable", "usb-c"] } } } )
- **Expected:** `usb-c` is already on A620 from insert — `$addToSet` leaves it unique. `portable` is added.

# Replace vs `$set` vs Upsert

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$set` keeps fields you did not mention
- `replaceOne` **drops** omitted fields (keeps `_id`)
- `upsert: true` updates or **inserts**
- `$setOnInsert` for fields only on insert
- Unique filter (`sku`) prevents duplicate upserts

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/103-field-update-vs-replacement.svg" alt="set versus replaceOne versus upsert" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Upsert Pattern

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Match found? Update the existing document
- No match? Insert a new document
- `$set` runs on **every** execution
- `$setOnInsert` runs **only** on insert (`createdAt`)
- Filter on unique `sku` so the second run updates

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/106-upsert-decision-flow.svg" alt="Match found updates; no match inserts" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 4.12 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.12`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.12-perform-an-upsert.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Run the upsert for a new SKU**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.updateOne( { sku: "A700" }, { $set: { name: "Portable Charger", category: "ACCESSORY", price: Decimal128("39.99"), active: true, updatedAt: new Date() }, $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date
- **Expected:** `upsertedId` is present. `createdAt` exists.

**Step 2 — Inspect the inserted document**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.findOne({ sku: "A700" })
- **Expected:** Fields from `$set` and `$setOnInsert` are present. Filter used the unique `sku`.

**Step 3 — Run the same upsert again**
- **Do:** Repeat the `updateOne` from Step 1, then `findOne` again.
- **Expected:** `matchedCount: 1`, `modifiedCount` may be 1 because `updatedAt` changes. `createdAt` must be **unchanged**. `upsertedId` is absent.

# Deleting Documents Safely

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `deleteOne` with a unique identifier
- `deleteMany` only after find + count + review
- `deleteMany({})` removes **all** documents
- Inspect `deletedCount`, then query again
- Consider **soft delete**: `active: false`, `deletedAt`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/112-safe-delete-workflow.svg" alt="Preview count delete verify sequence" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Soft Delete vs Hard Delete

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Hard: document is gone
- Soft: still queryable for audit
- Application reads add `{ active: true }`
- Never begin with an empty filter

</div>

<img src="assets/module-04/114-hard-vs-soft-delete.svg" alt="Hard delete versus soft delete" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 4.13 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.13`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.13-correct-unsafe-operations.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Unfiltered updateMany**
- **Do:** The unsafe command is: javascript db.products.updateMany({}, { $set: { active: false } })  Write the risk and a safer filter (for example discontinued items only). Do **not** run the unsafe command.
- **Expected:** Risk: every product becomes inactive. Safer: preview `{ tags: "discontinued" }` or `{ discontinuedAt: { $exists: true } }`, count, then `updateMany` with that f

**Step 2 — Empty deleteMany**
- **Do:** The unsafe command is: javascript db.orders.deleteMany({})  Write the risk and a safer sequence.
- **Expected:** Risk: all orders are removed. Safer: never use `{}`; filter on test `orderNumber` values; `find` → `countDocuments` → `deleteMany`.

**Step 3 — Replacing a nested object**
- **Do:** This update wipes sibling `contact` fields: javascript db.customers.updateOne( { customerNumber: "C101" }, { $set: { contact: { email: "new@example.com" } } } )  Rewrite it so only email changes.
- **Expected:** Safer: ```javascript db.customers.updateOne( { customerNumber: "C101" }, { $set: { "contact.email": "new@example.com" } } ) ```

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

# Bulk Write Operations

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `bulkWrite([ insertOne, updateOne, deleteOne, ... ])`
- Fewer application round trips
- Group related operations
- Still inspect the returned counts

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/117-bulk-write-overview.svg" alt="insert update and delete in one bulkWrite" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: Fewer application round trips.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Group related operations.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Still inspect the returned counts.

The figure on this slide is titled: insert update and delete in one bulkWrite.
-->

<!-- _class: content fit-xs -->

# Bulk Write Example

```javascript
db.products.bulkWrite([
  { insertOne: { document: { sku: "A600", name: "Wireless Presenter", category: "ACCESSORY", price: Decimal128("44.99"), active: true } } },
  { updateOne: { filter: { sku: "A400" }, update: { $set: { featured: true } } } },
  { deleteOne: { filter: { sku: "OLD-100" } } }
])
```

A400 already exists in the seed catalog. OLD-100 may match 0 documents — that is OK.

# Understanding Write Results

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Update: `acknowledged` `matchedCount` `modifiedCount` `upsertedId`
- Delete: `acknowledged` `deletedCount`
- `matchedCount: 1`, `modifiedCount: 0` — already that value
- `matchedCount: 0` — filter missed (types, case, db)

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/087-update-result-anatomy.svg" alt="How to read write results" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Atomicity and Concurrency

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- A write to **one document** is atomic
- Embed data that must change together
- Example: order status + total + line items
- Multi-document work may need transactions
- Transactions are a later, advanced topic

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/122-single-document-atomicity.svg" alt="Single document atomic versus multi-document" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Safe Update and Delete Practices

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Precise filters; unique ids when possible
- `find()` the filter before mass writes
- Correct BSON types; dotted nested paths
- Never start deletes with `{}`
- Soft delete + audit when policy requires
- Back up before true mass updates

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-04/128-safe-update-workflow.svg" alt="Safe update and delete rules" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Common Query Mistakes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Misspelled or wrong-case field names
- String dates / string money
- Unquoted dotted paths
- `$push` when uniqueness is required
- Omitting `$elemMatch`
- Mixed projections; broad write filters

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

## Exercise 4.14 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.14`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.14-diagnose-query-errors.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Wrong field capitalization**
- **Do:** This returns nothing: javascript db.products.find({ Category: "LAPTOP" })  Rewrite it.
- **Expected:** Field is `category` (lowercase). MongoDB does not fold identifier case.

**Step 2 — String instead of Decimal128**
- **Do:** This comparison is unreliable: javascript db.products.find({ price: { $gt: "100.00" } })  Rewrite it.
- **Expected:** Use `{ price: { $gt: Decimal128("100.00") } }`. Types must match stored BSON.

**Step 3 — Unquoted dotted path**
- **Do:** This is invalid: javascript db.products.find({ attributes.memoryGB: 16 })  Rewrite it.
- **Expected:** Quote the path: `{ "attributes.memoryGB": 16 }`.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

**Step 3 — Unquoted dotted path**
- **Do:** This is invalid: javascript db.products.find({ attributes.memoryGB: 16 })  Rewrite it.
- **Expected:** Quote the path: `{ "attributes.memoryGB": 16 }`.

- **Do:** This comparison is unreliable: ` db.products.find({ price: { $gt: "100.00" } }) ` Rewrite it.
- **Expected:** Use `{ price: { $gt: Decimal128("100.00") } }`. Types must match stored BSON.

- **Do:** Preview `{ sku: "A600" }` if you created it (otherwise use `A110`). `$set` `featured: true` and `updatedAt`. Inspect the write result and findOne.
- **Expected:** Four-part loop completed: preview, update, result, verify.

**Step 2 — $unset**
- **Do:** Add `temporaryNote` with `$set`, verify, then `$unset` it.
- **Expected:** Field is present after set and absent after unset.

**Step 3 — $inc**
- **Do:** `$inc` `stockQuantity` by 3 on that product.
- **Expected:** Quantity increased by exactly 3.

## Exercise 4.23 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 4.23`](../slide-exercises/module-04/exercise-4.23-lab-delete-operations.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Insert temporary documents**
- **Do:** insertMany products `TEMP-100` and `TEMP-101` with `labTag: "module4"` plus a throwaway order `TEMP-O1`.
- **Expected:** Two products and one order exist for this lab only.

**Step 2 — Build a precise deletion filter**
- **Do:** Use `{ sku: /^TEMP-/ }` or `{ labTag: "module4" }` — not `{}`.

<div class="cols">

- `$elemMatch` for one array element
- Update operators ≠ `replaceOne`
- Upsert may insert; unique filter required
- Verify every write

# Module Knowledge Check

1. `findOne()` vs `find()`?
2. What does `{}` match?
3. How do you query a nested field?
4. When is `$elemMatch` required?
5. Inclusion/exclusion projection rule?
6. `$push` vs `$addToSet`?
7. `updateOne()` vs `replaceOne()`?
8. What does `upsert: true` do?
9. `matchedCount: 1`, `modifiedCount: 0`?
10. Why preview a delete filter?
11. What does `deleteMany({})` do?
12. Why prefer `countDocuments()`?

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Find and project**
- **Do:** Find active products priced below Decimal128("80.00"). Project name, category, price, no `_id`. Record the count.
- **Expected:** A saved query plus the list you got.

- **Do:** Upsert sku `A900` (or a SKU the instructor assigns) with `$set` + `$setOnInsert` createdAt.
- **Expected:** Write result shows insert or update depending on prior labs.

- **Do:** `$addToSet` two tags; `$inc` stockQuantity.
- **Expected:** `modifiedCount` interpreted correctly on a second run.

# Operational Queries vs. Aggregation

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **find()** retrieves application records
- **aggregate()** transforms them into reports
- Stored fields versus calculated fields
- One filter versus ordered stages

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-05/001-operational-query-vs-aggregation.svg" alt="Operational query versus aggregation" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# Operational vs. aggregation — code

Operational:

```javascript
db.orders.find({ fulfillmentStatus: "SHIPPED" })
```

Analytical:

```javascript
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$fulfillmentStatus", orderCount: { $sum: 1 } } }
])
```

| Operational        | Aggregation              |
|--------------------|--------------------------|
| Retrieve documents | Transform documents      |
| Return stored fields | Calculate new fields   |
| Application lookup | Reporting and analysis   |

# What Is an Aggregation Pipeline?

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- An ordered list of processing stages
- Each stage receives documents
- Each stage performs one operation
- Output of one stage is input of the next

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-05/002-aggregation-pipeline-overview.svg" alt="Collection through stages to result" width="720">

</div>
</div>

- Final output is new documents

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Pipeline anatomy — code

```javascript
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { paymentStatus: "PAID" } },
  {
    $group: {
      _id: "$fulfillmentStatus",
      orderCount: { $sum: 1 },
      revenue: { $sum: "$total" }
    }
  },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }
])
```

<!-- _class: split -->

# How Documents Move Through a Pipeline

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Each stage’s output is the next stage’s input
- Documents are not updated in the collection
- A later stage never sees the original source shape unless you kept it

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-05/004-how-documents-move.svg" alt="Documents flowing from one stage to the next" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 5.1 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 5.1`](../slide-exercises/module-05/exercise-5.1-arrange-pipeline-stages.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Propose an order**
- **Do:** Write the six stages in the sequence you would run. Next to each stage, write one sentence on what the documents look like afterwards.
- **Expected:** A defensible sequence, not a guess. If two orders could work, note the trade-off.

**Step 2 — Check against the teaching pattern**
- **Do:** Compare your list with the instructor’s reveal: `$match` → `$unwind` → `$set` → `$group` → `$sort` → `$limit`.
- **Expected:** You can explain why `$limit` cannot come before `$sort`, and why `$unwind` must come before grouping by SKU.

# `$match` with Comparison Operators

```javascript
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { total: { $gte: Decimal128("500.00") } } }
])
```

Supported: `$eq` `$ne` `$gt` `$gte` `$lt` `$lte` `$in` `$nin`.

Money comparisons must use **Decimal128**, not `500` as a Double.

# `$match` with Logical Operators

```javascript
db.products.aggregate([
  {
    $match: {
      active: true,
      $or: [
        { category: "LAPTOP" },
        { category: "ACCESSORY" }
      ]
    }
  }
])
```

Comma-separated fields are AND. `$or` needs an array of expressions.

# Inclusion and Exclusion with `$project`

Inclusion:

```javascript
{ $project: { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 } }
```

Exclusion:

```javascript
{ $project: { attributes: 0, tags: 0 } }
```

Do not mix inclusion and exclusion except for `_id`.

# Renaming Fields with `$project`

```javascript
{ $project: {
    _id: 0,
    productCode: "$sku",
    productName: "$name",
    sellingPrice: "$price"
} }
```

The `$` prefix means “use the value from this field.” Without it, you store the literal string `sku`.

# Aggregation Expressions

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

# Field Reference Syntax

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `"category"` is the literal string category
- `"$category"` is the value of that field
- Forgetting `$` is the most common silent bug

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-05/030-field-reference-syntax.svg" alt="Dollar fieldName retrieves the current document value" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 1 on the slide: "category" is the literal string category.

Bullet 2 on the slide: "$category" is the value of that field.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Forgetting $ is the most common silent bug.

The figure on this slide is titled: Dollar fieldName retrieves the current document value.

<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# Arithmetic Expressions

`$add` `$subtract` `$multiply` `$divide` `$round`

```javascript
{ $project: {
    orderNumber: 1,
    calculatedLineTotal: {
      $multiply: ["$quantity", "$unitPrice"]
    }
} }
```

After `$unwind`, those fields are `$items.quantity` and `$items.unitPrice`.

<!--
The slide title is: Arithmetic Expressions.

The slide says: $add $subtract $multiply $divide $round.

The slide says: After $unwind, those fields are $items.quantity and $items.unitPrice.

The code on the slide reads: { $project: {     orderNumber: 1,     calculatedLineTotal: {       $multiply: ["$quantity", "$unitPrice"]     } } }.
-->

---












<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# String Expressions

`$concat` `$toUpper` `$toLower` `$trim` `$substrCP`

```javascript
{ $project: {
    customerName: {
      $concat: ["$name.first", " ", "$name.last"]
    }
} }
```

Missing first or last name yields null for the whole concat unless you `$ifNull` the parts.

<!--
The slide title is: String Expressions.

The slide says: $concat $toUpper $toLower $trim $substrCP.

The slide says: Missing first or last name yields null for the whole concat unless you $ifNull the parts.

The code on the slide reads: { $project: {     customerName: {       $concat: ["$name.first", " ", "$name.last"]     } } }.
-->

---












<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# Date Expressions

`$year` `$month` `$dayOfMonth` `$dayOfWeek` `$dateToString` `$dateTrunc`

```javascript
{ $set: {
    orderMonth: {
      $dateToString: { format: "%Y-%m", date: "$createdAt" }
    }
} }
```

Name a time zone in production reports.

# Conditional Expressions

`$cond` — two-way:

```javascript
{ $cond: [
  { $gte: ["$total", Decimal128("1000.00")] },
  "HIGH_VALUE",
  "STANDARD"
] }
```

`$switch` — several branches plus `default`. High-value paid orders in this set: O6101, O6202, O6301, O6304.

## Exercise 5.3 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 5.3`](../slide-exercises/module-05/exercise-5.3-reshape-documents-with-project.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Flat renamed projection**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.aggregate([ { $project: { _id: 0, productCode: "$sku", productName: "$name", category: 1, sellingPrice: "$price" } } ])
- **Expected:** Twelve documents. Fields are `productCode`, `productName`, `category`, `sellingPrice`. No `_id`.

**Step 2 — Nested output**
- **Do:** Run: javascript db.products.aggregate([ { $match: { sku: "L100" } }, { $project: { _id: 0, product: { code: "$sku", name: "$name" }, pricing: { amount: "$price" } } } ])
- **Expected:** One document: `product.code` is `L100`, `pricing.amount` is Decimal128 `1299.99`.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

# Accumulator Operators

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `$sum` `$avg` `$min` `$max`
- `$first` `$last` need a prior sort when order matters
- `$push` keeps duplicates; `$addToSet` unique values

</div>

</div>

# Counting, Sums, Averages, Min and Max

Count: `{ productCount: { $sum: 1 } }`

Revenue: `{ totalRevenue: { $sum: "$total" } }`

Average: `{ averagePrice: { $avg: "$price" } }`

Range: `{ minimumPrice: { $min: "$price" }, maximumPrice: { $max: "$price" } }`

Inputs must be compatible numeric types — Decimal128 for money.

<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# Preserving Values During Grouping

```javascript
{ $group: {
    _id: "$category",
    firstProduct: { $first: "$name" },
    productNames: { $push: "$name" },
    uniqueTags: { $addToSet: "$tags" }
} }
```

`$addToSet: "$tags"` collects **arrays of tags**, not individual tag strings. Flatten first if you need unique tag values.

- Need uniqueness? `$addToSet`

```javascript
    revenue: { $sum: "$total" }
} }
```

- **Expected:** Several combination documents. PAID + SHIPPED is a high-revenue group. PENDING + NEW includes O5001 and O6499.

# The `$sort`, `$limit`, and `$skip` Stages

Sort: `{ $sort: { totalRevenue: -1 } }` — add a tiebreaker for stable results.

Limit: `{ $limit: 5 }` — top N.

Skip: `{ $skip: 10 }` — basic paging; large skips are inefficient.

**Top-N pattern:** `$group` → `$sort` → `$limit`. Limit before sort is the wrong five documents.

- Limit then sort → an arbitrary subset, then ordered

# Document Multiplication Through `$unwind`

<div class="col-text">

- Pipeline count follows array lengths
- After unwind, `$sum: "$total"` repeats the order total

<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# Preserving Empty and Null Arrays

```javascript
{ $unwind: { path: "$items", preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true } }
```

Without this option, documents with missing, null, or empty `items` disappear.

Use it when the business still needs those parent documents.

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Working with Order Items

After `$unwind: "$items"`:

```javascript
{ $set: {
    lineRevenue: {
      $multiply: ["$items.quantity", "$items.unitPrice"]
    }
} }
{ $group: {
    _id: "$items.sku",
    unitsSold: { $sum: "$items.quantity" },
    revenue: { $sum: "$lineRevenue" }
} }
```

Do not `$sum: "$total"` after unwind — that repeats the **order** total on every line.

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Joining Customers and Orders

```javascript
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer"
  } },
  { $unwind: "$customer" },
  { $project: {
      _id: 0,
      orderNumber: 1,
      customerName: {
        $concat: ["$customer.name.first", " ", "$customer.name.last"]
      },
      total: 1
  } }
])
```

Plain `$unwind: "$customer"` **drops** O6499. Add `preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true` to keep it.

# Pipeline Variables

- `$fieldName` — current document field
- `$$variable` — defined variable
- `$$ROOT` — whole current document
- `$$CURRENT` — current processing context

```javascript
{ $map: {
    input: "$items",
    as: "item",
    in: { sku: "$$item.sku", quantity: "$$item.quantity" }
} }
```

`$filter` uses the same `$$item` convention.

# Daily, Monthly, and Yearly Grouping

`$dateToString` · `$dateTrunc` · `$year` · `$month` · `$dayOfMonth`

```javascript
{ $set: {
    month: { $dateTrunc: { date: "$createdAt", unit: "month" } }
} }
```

`$dateTrunc` returns a Date. `$dateToString` returns a sortable string. Pick one and stay consistent in the report.

# Pipeline Optimization Principles

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Filter early when possible
- Do not carry huge unused fields
- Control `$unwind` and `$lookup`
- Correctness before milliseconds

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-05/125-optimization-overview.svg" alt="Optimization practices" width="720">

</div>
</div>

- Late `$match` filters grouped results
- Both are valid — different questions

<div class="col-visual">

<!-- _class: split -->

# Early vs. Late `$match`

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Early: fewer documents enter expensive stages
- Late: you are filtering **groups**, not source rows
- Put source filters first; put summary filters after `$group`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-05/126-early-vs-late-match.svg" alt="Filtering before expensive stages versus processing extra documents" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The slide says: </div>.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Early: fewer documents enter expensive stages.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Late: you are filtering groups, not source rows.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Put source filters first; put summary filters after $group.

The figure on this slide is titled: Filtering before expensive stages versus processing extra documents.
-->

---












<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# `$project` Placement

Projection can shrink documents, but:

- Do not drop fields you still need
- MongoDB may optimize field use anyway
- Correctness and readability come first
- Final `$project` is for the report shape

Early `$unset` of `shippingAddress` is fine if no later stage needs it.

# Reading Aggregation Explain Output

```javascript
db.orders.explain("executionStats").aggregate([
  { $match: { paymentStatus: "PAID" } },
  { $sort: { createdAt: -1 } }
])
```

Look for: collection scan vs index scan, documents examined, keys examined, sort behavior, time.

Seventeen documents will not produce a dramatic speedup — read the **plan shape**.

<div class="cols">

- Grouping before unwind; summing order total per line

# Double-Counting After `$unwind`

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Parent `total` is copied onto every item row
- `$sum: "$total"` repeats the order once per SKU
- Sum line revenue instead: quantity × unitPrice

</div>

# Indexing and Query Performance

An index trades storage and write cost for faster access to selected data

The slide title is: Indexing and Query Performance.

The slide says: An index trades storage and write cost for faster access to selected data.

<!-- _class: content fit-md -->

# Module Learning Objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to:

- Recognize queries that need indexes
- Create, inspect, hide, and remove indexes
- Design compound indexes around query shapes
- Apply Equality–Sort–Range as a starting guideline
- Choose specialized index types appropriately
- Read essential `explain()` statistics
- Compare collection scans with index scans
- Remove unnecessary index overhead
- Recommend indexes based on evidence

# Why Query Performance Matters

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Slow user experiences and API timeouts
- More CPU and disk reads
- Higher cloud cost
- Resource contention
- Reduced system capacity
- Longer reporting jobs
- **Key:** one bad plan often hurts the whole workload

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/009-read-vs-write-cost.svg" alt="Faster reads balanced against write cost" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# How MongoDB Finds Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Without a suitable index, MongoDB may inspect many or all documents
- With a suitable index it can:
- 1. Navigate index keys
- 2. Identify candidate documents
- 3. Fetch only required records
- 4. Return matching results

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/006-index-lookup-flow.svg" alt="Query, index search, document references, results" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Collection Scan vs. Index Scan

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **COLLSCAN** — check documents in turn
- **IXSCAN** — search ordered keys, then selected documents
- **FETCH** — load full documents from index hits
- An index scan is not automatically efficient
- Examined keys and documents still matter

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/003-collscan-vs-ixscan.svg" alt="COLLSCAN versus IXSCAN" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# What Is an Index?

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- A separate, ordered data structure
- Stores values from indexed fields
- Stores references to documents
- Example key: category + price
- ACCESSORY | 49.99 → a product document

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/004-what-is-an-index.svg" alt="Ordered field values connected to documents" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Conceptual Index Structure

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Common indexes are conceptually tree-based and ordered
- Direct value lookup
- Ordered traversal
- Range lookup
- Sorted retrieval
- Prefix matching on compound keys
- Internal engine details are out of scope here

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/005-conceptual-index-structure.svg" alt="Tree-based navigation from a search key" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Index Benefits

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Equality and range searches
- Sorting and pagination
- Uniqueness enforcement
- Early aggregation `$match` / `$sort`
- `$lookup` on the foreign key
- Geospatial and text search
- TTL expiration of temporary data

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

</div>
</div>

# Index Costs and Tradeoffs

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Storage and memory pressure
- Insert, update, and delete cost
- Backup size and replication work
- Operational complexity
- **Key:** index real query patterns, not every field

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/008-index-costs.svg" alt="Storage, memory, write work, replication, maintenance" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# The Default `_id` Index

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Created automatically
- Fast `_id` lookups
- Enforces `_id` uniqueness
- Cannot normally be dropped on a regular collection
- Does **not** cover SKU, email, or orderNumber

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/012-business-id-vs-id.svg" alt="Automatic _id index versus SKU or order-number indexes" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Creating an Index

```javascript
db.products.createIndex({ sku: 1 })
```

With a custom name:

```javascript
db.products.createIndex(
  { sku: 1 },
  { name: "idx_products_sku" }
)
```

`1` is ascending; `-1` is descending. **Name indexes on purpose.**

# Hiding and Unhiding an Index

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Still stored and maintained
- Planner will not select it
- `hideIndex` / `unhideIndex`
- Test whether the index is still required
- **Tradeoff:** writes and storage still paid

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/126-hidden-vs-dropped.svg" alt="Reversible planner exclusion compared with physical removal" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Single-Field Indexes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `{ category: 1 }` supports `find({ category: "LAPTOP" })`
- May also support sorting by that field
- Strong candidate: unique business identifiers
- Weak standalone candidate: booleans

</div>

# Ascending and Descending Index Direction

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Single-field indexes can usually be traversed either way
- `{ createdAt: 1 }` can serve `sort({ createdAt: 1 })` and reverse
- Direction matters more on compound indexes with mixed sorts

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/016-ascending-vs-descending.svg" alt="Direction on single-field versus compound indexes" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Compound Indexes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- More than one field in one index
- `{ category: 1, price: 1 }`
- May support equality plus a range on the later field
- One well-ordered compound index often beats two single-field indexes

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<!-- _class: split -->

# Compound-Index Prefixes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- For `{ category: 1, price: 1, name: 1 }`
- Usable: category
- Usable: category + price
- Usable: category + price + name
- A query on price alone does not use that leading prefix
- **Key:** leftmost fields organize the index

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/021-compound-index-prefixes.svg" alt="Left-to-right compound prefixes" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Indexes for Equality, Range, and Sort

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Equality: jump to matching keys — `{ sku: 1 }`
- Range: scan a key interval — `{ price: 1 }`
- Sort: traverse already-ordered keys
- Equality on a leading field lets the next field provide order

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/026-classifying-esr-fields.svg" alt="Equality, range, and sort index behavior" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Sort Direction and Index Direction

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Complete reverse `{ category: -1, price: 1 }` can use the same index
- Arbitrary mixed directions may add a SORT stage

## Exercise 6.3 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 6.3`](../slide-exercises/module-06/exercise-6.3-arrange-compound-fields.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Label ESR roles**
- **Do:** Given: javascript db.orders .find({ customerId: customerId, paymentStatus: "PAID", total: { $gte: Decimal128("500.00") } }) .sort({ createdAt: -1 })  Label each field as equality, sort, or range.
- **Expected:** Equality: customerId, paymentStatus. Sort: createdAt. Range: total.

- **Do:** Write a candidate key following Equality–Sort–Range. Then note when you might put the more selective equality field first if `paymentStatus` is a small set of values.
- **Expected:** Candidate `{ customerId: 1, paymentStatus: 1, createdAt: -1, total: 1 }`. Alternative: still lead with customerId (high selectivity) even if paymentStatus is lo

- **Expected:** `{ paymentStatus: 1, createdAt: -1 }`. Equality first partitions the index so the date sort/range walks one status’s keys instead of mixing statuses.

Bullet 15 on the slide: Do: Shape C: paymentStatus PAID, createdAt ≥ start, sort createdAt descending. Propose an index and one sentence on why paymentStatus still belongs first even though it is low selectivity.

Bullet 16 on the slide: Expected: { paymentStatus: 1, createdAt: -1 }. Equality first partitions the index so the date sort/range walks one status’s keys instead of mixing statuses.

## Exercise 6.5 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 6.5`](../slide-exercises/module-06/exercise-6.5-identify-index-prefixes.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — List usable prefixes**
- **Do:** Given `{ customerId: 1, paymentStatus: 1, createdAt: -1 }`, list the prefixes MongoDB can use from the left.
- **Expected:** customerId; customerId + paymentStatus; customerId + paymentStatus + createdAt.

**Step 2 — Mark unsupported shapes**
- **Do:** Decide whether these can use that index as a leading prefix: (1) filter only paymentStatus, (2) filter customerId, (3) filter customerId and sort createdAt without paymentStatus.
- **Expected:** (1) No — paymentStatus is not leading. (2) Yes. (3) Usually not for the sort: skipping paymentStatus breaks the sort prefix, so an extra SORT is likely.

# Multikey Indexes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- An array-valued indexed path creates an entry per element
- `{ tags: 1 }` supports `find({ tags: "technology" })`
- The index is reported as multikey
- Array cardinality multiplies index keys

</div>

</div>
</div>

# Partial Indexes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Index only documents matching a filter
- Example: `partialFilterExpression: { active: true }`
- Smaller index, lower maintenance
- Queries generally need to be compatible with the filter

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/047-partial-vs-sparse.svg" alt="Partial versus sparse selection rules" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Sparse Indexes

A sparse index omits documents that **do not contain** the indexed field.

```javascript
db.products.createIndex(
  { discountCode: 1 },
  { sparse: true }
)
```

Less flexible than a partial index: the rule is only “field exists,” not an arbitrary filter.

<!--
The slide title is: Sparse Indexes.

The slide says: A sparse index omits documents that do not contain the indexed field.

The slide says: Less flexible than a partial index: the rule is only “field exists,” not an arbitrary filter.

The code on the slide reads: db.products.createIndex(   { discountCode: 1 },   { sparse: true } ).
-->

---












<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Partial vs. Sparse Indexes

| Consideration | Partial | Sparse |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Selection rule | Explicit filter | Indexed field exists |
| Flexibility | Higher | Lower |
| Common use | Active / status subset | Optional field |
| Query compatibility | Must align with filter | Respect missing fields |

**Preference:** partial when you can state the subset clearly.

# TTL Indexes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Expire documents from a date field
- `expireAfterSeconds: 0` with an `expiresAt` timestamp
- Sessions, tokens, short-lived logs, cache rows
- Expiration is **asynchronous**, not exact-timestamp

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/048-ttl-index.svg" alt="TTL index lifecycle" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Text, Wildcard, Geospatial, and Hashed

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Text:** `$text` word search — one text index per collection
- **Wildcard:** `attributes.$**` for dynamic paths
- **Geospatial:** `2dsphere` on GeoJSON points
- **Hashed:** equality distribution; no ordered range
- Advanced search often belongs in a dedicated search product

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/037-index-types-overview.svg" alt="Specialized index types" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Text and Wildcard Examples

```javascript
db.products.createIndex({ name: "text", description: "text" })
db.products.find({ $text: { $search: "wireless keyboard" } })

db.products.createIndex({ "attributes.$**": 1 })
```

training_store product `attributes` vary by category (laptop vs shoe vs book). Wildcard can index those paths; it is still a write and storage cost.

<!--
The slide title is: Text and Wildcard Examples.

The slide says: training_store product attributes vary by category (laptop vs shoe vs book). Wildcard can index those paths; it is still a write and storage cost.

The code on the slide reads: db.products.createIndex({ name: "text", description: "text" }) db.products.find({ $text: { $search: "wireless keyboard" } }) db.products.createIndex({ "attributes.$**": 1 }).
-->

---












<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Geospatial and Hashed Examples

```javascript
db.stores.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" })
```

Use for nearby stores, delivery zones, asset locations.

```javascript
db.events.createIndex({ tenantId: "hashed" })
```

Hashed keys support hashed sharding and equality distribution. They do **not** preserve sort order or range scans.

# Choosing the Appropriate Index Type

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- One field lookup → single-field
- Filter and sort on several fields → compound
- Unique identifier → unique
- Array elements → multikey
- Active subset → partial
- Expire rows → TTL
- Dynamic attributes → wildcard (with caution)

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/038-index-type-selection-map.svg" alt="Requirement to index-type mapping" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Covered Queries

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- All filter fields are in the index
- All returned fields are in the index
- MongoDB does not need to FETCH full documents
- Exclude `_id` if it is not in the index
- Confirm with `explain()` — do not assume

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/072-covered-vs-noncovered.svg" alt="Conditions for a covered query" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Index Selectivity

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Higher:** email, SKU, order number
- **Lower:** `active`, small status sets, a few countries
- Low-selectivity fields still help in compound or partial indexes
- A leading boolean can make an IXSCAN almost a COLLSCAN

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/078-high-vs-low-selectivity.svg" alt="High versus low selectivity fields" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Sort fields and projection
- Collation and query options
- Same shape → same index design
- Index recurring shapes, not isolated example values

# Index Intersection

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- MongoDB may combine two single-field indexes
- `{ category: 1 }` and `{ active: 1 }`
- A designed compound index is usually more predictable
- Especially when a sort is required

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/087-intersection-vs-compound.svg" alt="Index intersection versus a compound index" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Indexes and Regular Expressions

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Anchored prefix `^Mongo` may use an index
- Unanchored `/Mongo/` often scans broadly
- Leading wildcards, case, and collation change eligibility
- Do not use regex as a substitute for a structured field

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/069-prefix-regex-index.svg" alt="Anchored versus unanchored regular expressions" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Indexes, Aggregation, and `$lookup`

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Helpful early: `$match`, `$sort`, some geo stages
- Paid orders newest first → `{ paymentStatus: 1, createdAt: -1 }`
- `$group` still runs after the indexed prefix
- `$lookup`: index the **foreign** field
- `customers._id` is already indexed

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

# Using `explain()`

```javascript
db.products.find({ category: "ACCESSORY" }).explain("executionStats")

db.products.explain("executionStats").find({ category: "ACCESSORY" })

db.orders.explain("executionStats").aggregate([
  { $match: { paymentStatus: "PAID" } }
])
```

<div class="col-text">

- **executionStats** — adds nReturned, keys, docs, timing
- **allPlansExecution** — candidate race during selection
- Training default: `executionStats`

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Reading `queryPlanner` and `executionStats`

**queryPlanner — ask:**

- Expected index or COLLSCAN?
- Extra SORT?
- Which candidates were rejected?

**executionStats — record:**

- `nReturned`
- `totalKeysExamined`
- `totalDocsExamined`
- Stage tree and execution-time indicators

**Healthy direction:** examined counts stay close to the data the query actually needs.

# `COLLSCAN` vs `IXSCAN` vs `FETCH`

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- COLLSCAN — collection documents
- IXSCAN — index keys
- FETCH — documents after index hits
- Common: IXSCAN → FETCH → result
- Covered: IXSCAN → projection → result

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/076-ixscan-projection-vs-fetch.svg" alt="Stage flow for indexed and covered queries" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Examined vs. Returned Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- 100,000 examined / 10 returned → high scan cost
- 10 keys / 10 docs / 10 returned → targeted
- Ratios are signals, not SLAs
- training_store numbers stay small — still record them

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

# In-Memory Sort Indicators

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- If the index cannot provide order, MongoDB adds SORT
- More CPU and memory
- Higher latency
- Large sorts may spill depending on configuration
- A matching compound index may remove the extra sort

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/063-index-vs-inmemory-sort.svg" alt="Index-provided order versus extra SORT" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Over-Indexing

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Slow inserts and updates
- Large index storage and memory pressure
- Longer maintenance operations
- Many similar indexes
- Indexes with no corresponding query
- The right number is workload-dependent

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

# Indexes and Write Performance

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Each insert updates the document, `_id`, and every affected secondary index
- More indexes → more write work
- Updates to indexed fields cost more than updates to non-indexed fields

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/118-insert-with-multiple-indexes.svg" alt="Write path touching document and indexes" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Storage and Working Memory

**Index size depends on:** document count, key size, field count, array cardinality, index count, value repetition, and type.

Monitor collection data size **and** total index size.

Frequently used index pages may stay in memory. If the working set exceeds RAM:

- Disk access rises
- Latency becomes less predictable
- Competing queries evict useful pages

Smaller, targeted indexes are easier to keep hot.

- Names should state operational intent

# Production Index-Change Safety

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Capture the query shape and baseline explain
- Estimate size and build impact
- Test in a representative environment
- Schedule or control the change
- Monitor query and write latency; check replication
- Keep a rollback path and document the reason

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

</div>
</div>

# Query-Tuning Workflow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Identify the slow operation and exact shape
- Baseline + `explain("executionStats")`
- Check types and predicates
- Smallest useful index
- Create or hide-test; re-explain
- Compare examined keys and documents
- Check write/storage impact; monitor under load

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-06/131-query-tuning-lifecycle.svg" alt="Query-tuning workflow" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Common Indexing Mistakes

- Indexing every field
- Ignoring compound-field order
- Creating duplicate / overlapping indexes
- Placing a range field too early
- Ignoring sort requirements
- Indexing low-selectivity fields without context
- Indexing a one-time query
- Ignoring write overhead
- Assuming every `IXSCAN` is efficient
- Not verifying with `explain()`
- Removing an index without dependency analysis
- Ignoring data types and collation

# Index Troubleshooting Workflow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Confirm database, collection, filter types
- Inspect the winning plan and eligibility
- Review prefixes and sort compatibility
- Check keys/docs examined and result size
- Consider multikey expansion and working-set size
- Compare against production-like data

</div>

# E-Commerce Indexing Strategy

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- SKU → unique `{ sku: 1 }`
- Catalog → `{ category: 1, active: 1, price: 1 }`
- Tags → multikey `{ tags: 1 }`
- Email → `{ "contact.email": 1 }`
- Order number → unique
- History → `{ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 }`
- Paid reports → `{ paymentStatus: 1, createdAt: -1 }`
- Sessions → TTL on `expiresAt`

</div>

# Module Summary

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Indexes speed selected reads and tax writes/storage
- Compound order and prefixes define supported shapes
- ESR is a starting guideline
- Arrays become multikey; specialized types solve specific jobs
- `explain()` is evidence; IXSCAN is not a trophy
- Hide, measure, maintain

## Exercise 6.11 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 6.11`](../slide-exercises/module-06/exercise-6.11-correct-indexing-anti-patterns.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Correct the first four**
- **Do:** Rewrite: index every field; one new index per query without checking overlap; put a range field first in every compound index; drop unused indexes immediately.
- **Expected:** Index recurring query shapes. Reuse prefixes. Equality (then sort) before range. Hide, measure, then drop.

**Step 2 — Correct the last three**
- **Do:** Rewrite: treat every IXSCAN as optimal; ignore write overhead; design indexes only on development-sized data.
- **Expected:** Read examined keys/docs. Count secondary indexes on the write path. Validate with production-like volume and distribution.

_Full lab guide with every command: see **Lab guide** on the lesson divider slide._

# Exercise 6.12 — Build an Indexing Recommendation

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

## Lab 6.4 — Steps 3–4



**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 3 — Compare a worse order**
- **Do:** Create `{ createdAt: -1, customerId: 1 }` as `idx_orders_created_customer` only if you have time, explain the same query, then drop that experimental index.
- **Expected:** Leading with the range/sort field scans more keys across customers. Evidence favors customerId first. Drop the experimental index.

**Step 4 — Choose and document**
- **Do:** Keep idx_orders_customer_created. Write why ESR put equality first here.
- **Expected:** A short justification: one customer’s keys are contiguous, then dates are ordered for newest-first and the range.

## Exercise 6.13 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 6.13`](../slide-exercises/module-06/exercise-6.13-practical-challenge.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Tabulate ten patterns**
- **Do:** For each workload item (SKU lookup, category browse, tags, email, order number, order history, paid reporting, reviews newest first, session expiration, dynamic attributes), write query shape and a proposed index.
- **Expected:** A ten-row table exists. Unique, multikey, partial, TTL, and wildcard candidates are marked.

**Step 2 — Justify field order and costs**
- **Do:** For every compound index, state ESR roles and one write/storage sentence. Flag any overlapping prefixes (for example category vs category+active+price).
- **Expected:** Compound orders are justified. At least one overlap is called out with a retain/hide plan.

**Step 3 — Validation plan**
- **Do:** Write how you would prove two high-traffic indexes with explain (catalog and order history) and how you would roll back.
- **Expected:** Baseline → createIndex → executionStats comparison → dropIndex rollback with the original createIndex saved.

# Transition to Module 7: Replication and Sharding

Module 7 moves from individual query performance to distributed availability and scale:

- Replica-set architecture
- Primary and secondary members
- Elections and automatic failover
- Read and write concerns
- Sharding architecture and shard keys
- Routers and configuration servers
- Balancing and data distribution
- Replication versus sharding
- High-availability and scaling decisions

Hashed indexes you saw today reappear as hashed shard keys.

# Availability and Scalability Requirements

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Remain available during server failure
- Recover from infrastructure problems
- Handle growing data and request volume
- Serve users in multiple locations
- Meet durability and latency objectives
- Start from business requirements, not hardware

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/02-requirements.svg" alt="Business needs mapped to availability and scale" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# High Availability vs. Horizontal Scalability

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **High availability:** service stays accessible during component failure
- MongoDB mechanism: **replica sets**
- **Horizontal scalability:** spread data and workload
- MongoDB mechanism: **sharding**
- Need both: **sharded replica sets**

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/03-ha-vs-scale.svg" alt="Replica sets for HA, sharding for scale" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Requirement to mechanism

| Requirement | Main mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Server redundancy | Replication |
| Automatic failover | Replication |
| More storage capacity | Sharding |
| More distributed throughput | Sharding |
| Availability and scale | Sharded replica sets |

<!-- _class: split -->

# Vertical Scaling vs. Horizontal Scaling

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Vertical:** more CPU, RAM, disk, faster storage on one server
- Usually simpler — until the box or the bill stops you
- **Horizontal:** more servers, distributed work
- Broader growth, more operational complexity
- Indexing and schema work come before sharding

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/04-vertical-horizontal.svg" alt="Bigger box versus more boxes" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Replication vs. Sharding

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Replication **copies** the same logical dataset
- Sharding **partitions** data across shards
- Replica set: primary + secondaries, failover
- Sharded cluster: multiple shards, distributed traffic
- Production shards are normally replica sets

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/05-replication-vs-sharding.svg" alt="Copy versus partition" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# MongoDB Distributed Architecture Overview

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Application → driver → query router
- Router sends work to the right shard
- Each shard is typically a replica set
- Config servers hold cluster metadata
- Distributed data, distributed work, local redundancy

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/06-distributed-overview.svg" alt="App, mongos, three sharded replica sets" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 7.1 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 7.1`](../slide-exercises/module-07/exercise-7.1-replication-or-sharding.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Classify six requirements**
- **Do:** For each item, write **Replication**, **Sharding**, **Both**, or **Neither yet**: (1) survive one server failure, (2) increase total data capacity, (3) automatically elect a replacement primary, (4) distribute write load

- **Do:** In two sentences, explain why copying data to secondaries does **not** increase total storage capacity for the application dataset.
- **Expected:** Each member stores the same logical dataset. Extra members add redundancy, not a larger working set.

# What Is a Replica Set?

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- A group of `mongod` processes with the same dataset
- Common shape: one primary, two or more secondaries
- Odd number of voting members where practical
- Provides redundancy, election, failover, maintenance windows

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/07-replica-set.svg" alt="Primary and two secondaries" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Replica-Set Members

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Primary, secondary, hidden, delayed
- Non-voting members and (rarely) arbiters
- Not every member must serve application reads
- Roles are configuration, not personality

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/08-members.svg" alt="Member roles table" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Primary Member Responsibilities

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Accepts application writes
- Applies writes and records the oplog
- Participates in elections
- Serves reads under `primary` read preference
- Only one primary at a time in the set

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/09-primary.svg" alt="Primary write and oplog path" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Secondary Member Responsibilities

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Maintains a copy of the data
- Copies and applies oplog operations in order
- Eligible secondaries can become primary
- May serve reads when read preference allows
- An active participant, not a tape backup

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/10-secondary.svg" alt="Copy, apply, maybe elect" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# The Replication Oplog

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- A capped collection of data-changing operations
- Primary writes an entry after applying the change
- Secondaries copy entries and apply them
- The oplog window must cover how long a member can be down

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/11-oplog.svg" alt="Write, oplog, copy, apply" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Replication Data Flow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Driver discovers the current primary
- Application write → primary apply → oplog
- Secondaries retrieve and apply
- Client acknowledgment follows **write concern**

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/12-replication-flow.svg" alt="Driver, primary, secondaries, ack" width="720">

</div>
</div>

**Step 1 — Label members and clients**
- **Do:** On the replica-set diagram, mark Application, Driver, Primary, and two Secondaries.
- **Expected:** One primary, two secondaries, client path through the driver — not a raw single-host arrow to a secondary for writes.

**Step 2 — Label flows**
- **Do:** Draw oplog flow (primary → secondaries), heartbeats (all members), write path (app → primary), and a primary-preference read path.
- **Expected:** Writes hit the primary. Heartbeats are separate from oplog copy. Reads to secondaries are not the default write path.

# Exercise 7.3 — Trace a Replicated Write

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Time:** 15 min
- Sequence a write from the client through oplog apply and write-concern ack.

## Exercise 7.3 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 7.3`](../slide-exercises/module-07/exercise-7.3-trace-a-replicated-write.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Order the seven events**
- **Do:** Number these 1–7: client sends write; driver selects primary; primary applies write; oplog entry is created; secondaries copy the operation; secondaries apply it; acknowledgment returns based on write concern.
- **Expected:** That listed order is the teaching sequence. Acknowledgment is last and depends on `w`.

**Step 2 — Change one setting**
- **Do:** State what changes if write concern is majority instead of primary-only acknowledgment.
- **Expected:** The client waits until a majority of voting data-bearing members have durably acknowledged, so latency can increase and durability confidence increases.

# Replica-Set Heartbeats

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Members exchange regular health information
- Who is reachable, who is primary, who may vote
- Whether an election may be required
- Heartbeats do **not** copy application data

# Replica-Set Elections

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Network or config changes that affect majority
- A better eligible candidate (priority)
- Eligible voting members choose a new primary

</div>

# Automatic Failover

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Failure detected → election → new primary
- Writes may pause during the election
- Some reads may be affected
- Drivers rediscover topology; retries help

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

</div>

# Application Behavior During Failover

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Use a replica-set connection string
- Use a supported driver and sensible timeouts
- Retry eligible operations; handle transients
- Do not pin forever to one hostname
- Make critical writes idempotent

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

# Majority and Voting Concepts

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Need a voting majority to elect and keep a primary
- Three voters: two are a majority
- One isolated member cannot elect itself
- Partitions follow the majority side — avoids two primaries

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/17-majority.svg" alt="Two of three form a majority" width="720">

</div>

# Replica-Set Member Priorities

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Priority influences who becomes primary
- Prefer a member in the primary data center
- Keep a reporting node from becoming primary
- Not a performance router for ordinary reads

</div>

# Arbiter Overview and Limitations

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Votes in elections; stores **no** application data
- Cannot become primary; adds no copy and no read capacity
- Use only after understanding durability and security tradeoffs
- A data-bearing voter is usually more valuable

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/19-arbiter.svg" alt="Arbiter cannot store data" width="720">

- Can be blocked from becoming primary

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Primary Read Preference

`primary` sends reads to the current primary.

**Advantages**

- Sees the primary’s current state
- Simplest consistency story
- Default for many workloads

**Tradeoff**

- Reads share primary resources with writes
- Reads can pause briefly during elections

---












<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Secondary Read Preferences

Secondary reads may help reporting, geo-local reads, or shedding some primary read load.

**Tradeoffs**

- Data may be behind the primary
- Stale results can be wrong for the business
- Secondary capacity is not free

Sending reads to secondaries does **not** automatically make the whole system faster.

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Number of acks, majority, journal, timeout
- Controls durability confidence vs latency

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Common Write-Concern Levels

**Primary acknowledgment (`w: 1`)**  
Lower latency, less replica-set confirmation.

**Majority**  
A majority of voting data-bearing members have acknowledged per configured semantics.

**Custom numeric `w`**  
Wait for N members.

Stronger acknowledgment usually increases durability confidence and can increase latency. Do not present `w: 0` / `w: 1` as a universal performance solution.

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Read Concern

Influences visibility and isolation of reads.

Common levels: `local` · `available` · `majority` · `linearizable` · `snapshot`

Choose based on transactions, staleness tolerance, performance, deployment, and application semantics.

This module teaches the **idea**. Exact guarantees depend on version and topology — confirm in docs for production.

# Replication Lag

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Delay between apply on primary and apply on a secondary
- Affects secondary-read freshness
- Affects failover readiness
- Affects recovery and oplog-window planning

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/25-lag.svg" alt="Primary T0 versus secondary T0 plus lag" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The figure on this slide is titled: Primary T0 versus secondary T0 plus lag.

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Causes of Replication Lag

- Slow disks, network latency, insufficient CPU
- Heavy write volume or large operations
- Index differences and resource contention
- Maintenance and secondary-specific workloads
- Oplog window too small for an interrupted member

Lag is a **symptom**. Collect disk, CPU, network, currentOps, and oplog window before you rebuild a node.

# Rollback Concepts

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Former primary has writes not on the new authoritative history
- MongoDB reconciles that member with the current primary
- Reduce risk: majority writes, stable networks, correct drivers
- Rollback is not “the database randomly deletes orders for fun”

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/26-rollback.svg" alt="Former primary versus current history" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Replica-Set Operational Practices

- Odd number of voting members where practical
- Independent failure domains
- Monitor lag and oplog window
- Replica-set connection strings
- Test failover; keep backups
- Appropriate read and write concerns
- Consistent member config; secure member and client traffic

<!-- _class: split -->

# Replica-Set Failure Scenarios

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **One secondary down:** primary usually stays writable; repair soon
- **Primary down, majority up:** election; brief write pause
- **Majority unavailable:** no writable primary — consistency wins
- Administrator intervention may be required in the last case

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/28-failure-scenarios.svg" alt="Three failure outcomes" width="720">

</div>
</div>

**Step 1 — Map five symptoms**
- **Do:** For each: high disk latency; heavy reporting on a secondary; network congestion; rapid write growth; small oplog window — write likely cause, impact, evidence to collect, and first action.
- **Expected:** Disk: storage saturation → growing lag → iostat/Atlas metrics → faster disks or less write amplification. Reporting: secondary CPU/IO → lag + stale reads → isol

**Step 2 — Pick the first metric**
- **Do:** If a secondary is 90 seconds behind and reporting dashboards look empty, which two checks do you run first?
- **Expected:** `rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()` / member optimes, and secondary CPU, disk, and current operations — not an immediate rebuild.

Bullet 16 on the slide: Expected: rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo() / member optimes, and secondary CPU, disk, and current operations — not an immediate rebuild.
-->

## Lab 7.1 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Lab 7.1`](../slide-exercises/module-07/lab-7.1-verify-replica-set-health.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Confirm you are on a replica set**
- **Do:** Connect with the replica-set / Atlas URI, then run: ` rs.status() rs.conf() `
- **Expected:** A replica-set name, one `PRIMARY`, one or more `SECONDARY` members, `health: 1` on reachable members. If you see a standalone error, stop and switch URI.

**Step 2 — Record identity and votes**
- **Do:** From `rs.status()` and `rs.conf()`, write: set name, primary host, secondary hosts, each member’s `votes` and `priority`. Note any arbiter.
- **Expected:** A table of members with state, votes, and priority. Atlas typically shows three data-bearing members and no arbiter.

# What Is Sharding?

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Partitions a collection across multiple shards
- Each shard stores only part of the sharded dataset
- Supports storage, query, and write scale
- Adds significant operational complexity

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/29-what-is-sharding.svg" alt="Three shards holding ranges" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — What Is Sharding?.

The slide title is: What Is Sharding?.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Partitions a collection across multiple shards.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Each shard stores only part of the sharded dataset.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Supports storage, query, and write scale.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Adds significant operational complexity.

The figure on this slide is titled: Three shards holding ranges.
-->

---












<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Why Applications Need Sharding

Consider sharding when:

- Dataset exceeds one replica set’s practical capacity
- Read or write demand exceeds one replica set
- Working set no longer fits effectively
- Geographic placement is required
- Vertical scaling is no longer sustainable

**Warning:** shard to a measured need, not a slide from a conference.

# Shards

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Each shard holds a subset of sharded data
- Production shard = replica set
- Partitioned data plus redundancy inside the partition
- Independent failover for that shard’s members

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/31-shards.svg" alt="Shard as replica set" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Each shard holds a subset of sharded data.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Production shard = replica set.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Partitioned data plus redundancy inside the partition.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Independent failover for that shard’s members.

The figure on this slide is titled: Shard as replica set.
-->

# Configuration Server Replica Set

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Stores cluster metadata: collections, keys, ranges, zones
- Critical infrastructure — availability and backups matter
- Not where `orders` documents live

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/32-csrs.svg" alt="Config metadata kinds" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# The `mongos` Query Router

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Accepts client requests and reads metadata
- Targets shards; merges results when needed
- Does **not** store application collection data
- Deploy more than one router for applications

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/33-mongos.svg" alt="mongos routing steps" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Sharded Request Flow

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- App → `mongos` interprets the query
- `mongos` consults routing metadata
- Relevant shard or shards execute
- Merge if required, then reply

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/34-request-flow.svg" alt="Request flow through mongos" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# What Is a Shard Key?

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Field or fields used to distribute documents
- `{ customerId: 1 }`
- `{ tenantId: 1, createdAt: 1 }`
- `{ customerId: "hashed" }`
- One of the most important sharding decisions

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/35-shard-key.svg" alt="Example shard keys" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Shard-Key Characteristics

Evaluate:

- Cardinality and frequency distribution
- Write distribution and query targeting
- Growth pattern and divisibility
- Locality and long-term application behavior

There is **no** universally ideal shard key.

<!--
This slide lists key points under Shard-Key Characteristics.

The slide title is: Shard-Key Characteristics.

The slide says: Evaluate:.

The slide says: There is no universally ideal shard key.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Cardinality and frequency distribution.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Write distribution and query targeting.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Growth pattern and divisibility.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Locality and long-term application behavior.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Cardinality

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Low:** NEW, PAID, SHIPPED — too few buckets
- **High:** customerId, orderId, deviceId
- Higher cardinality enables finer distribution
- Still check frequency — one celebrity customer

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/36-cardinality.svg" alt="Low versus high cardinality" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Cardinality.

The slide title is: Cardinality.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Low: NEW, PAID, SHIPPED — too few buckets.

Bullet 2 on the slide: High: customerId, orderId, deviceId.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Higher cardinality enables finer distribution.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Still check frequency — one celebrity customer.

The figure on this slide is titled: Low versus high cardinality.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Frequency and Value Distribution

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- High cardinality can still skew
- Tenant A = 80% of traffic → hot shard
- Uneven storage and request load
- Use real workload patterns, not unique-count only

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/37-frequency.svg" alt="Skewed tenant traffic" width="720">

</div>
</div>

This slide includes a diagram — Frequency and Value Distribution.

Bullet 1 on the slide: High cardinality can still skew.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Tenant A = 80% of traffic → hot shard.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Uneven storage and request load.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Use real workload patterns, not unique-count only.

The figure on this slide is titled: Skewed tenant traffic.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Monotonic Shard Keys

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Increasing timestamps, sequences, counters
- Ranged sharding sends new writes to the high end
- Creates a write hotspot on one chunk/shard
- Mitigate: hashed, compound, other distribution, careful zones

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/38-monotonic.svg" alt="Writes piling on the max range" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Monotonic Shard Keys.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Increasing timestamps, sequences, counters.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Ranged sharding sends new writes to the high end.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Creates a write hotspot on one chunk/shard.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Mitigate: hashed, compound, other distribution, careful zones.

The figure on this slide is titled: Writes piling on the max range.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Query Isolation

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- A query is targeted when the router can pick shard(s) from the key
- `find({ customerId: "C101" })` if customerId is the key
- Without a usable key predicate, the query goes broadly

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/39-query-isolation.svg" alt="Targeted versus untargeted find" width="720">

</div>
</div>

This slide includes a diagram — Query Isolation.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: A query is targeted when the router can pick shard(s) from the key.

Bullet 2 on the slide: find({ customerId: "C101" }) if customerId is the key.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Without a usable key predicate, the query goes broadly.

The figure on this slide is titled: Targeted versus untargeted find.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Ranged Sharding

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Contiguous key ranges: A–F, G–M, N–Z
- Efficient range targeting and locality
- Risks: uneven values, monotonic write hotspots

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/40-ranged.svg" alt="Alphabet ranges on three shards" width="720">

</div>
</div>

This slide includes a diagram — Ranged Sharding.

The slide title is: Ranged Sharding.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Contiguous key ranges: A–F, G–M, N–Z.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Efficient range targeting and locality.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Risks: uneven values, monotonic write hotspots.

The figure on this slide is titled: Alphabet ranges on three shards.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Hashed Sharding

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Hash the key, then range the hashes
- Even distribution for many equality workloads
- Reduces monotonic concentration
- Range queries often hit many shards; locality lost

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/41-hashed.svg" alt="Value to hash to shard" width="720">

</div>
</div>

This slide includes a diagram — Hashed Sharding.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Hash the key, then range the hashes.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Even distribution for many equality workloads.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Reduces monotonic concentration.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Range queries often hit many shards; locality lost.

The figure on this slide is titled: Value to hash to shard.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Zoned Sharding

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Associate key ranges with particular shards
- Geo placement, residency, hardware tiers, tenants
- Canada ranges → Canada zone; Europe → Europe zone
- Requires careful operational planning

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/42-zoned.svg" alt="Canada and Europe zones" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: Geo placement, residency, hardware tiers, tenants.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Canada ranges → Canada zone; Europe → Europe zone.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Requires careful operational planning.

The figure on this slide is titled: Canada and Europe zones.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Ranged vs. Hashed Sharding

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Ranged: order, range queries, locality, hotspot risk
- Hashed: even spread, sequential-write relief, scatter ranges
- Pick from the query mix, not from fashion

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/43-ranged-vs-hashed.svg" alt="Ranged versus hashed comparison" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: Hashed: even spread, sequential-write relief, scatter ranges.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Pick from the query mix, not from fashion.

The figure on this slide is titled: Ranged versus hashed comparison.
-->

---












<!-- _class: split -->

# Compound Shard Keys

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- `{ tenantId: 1, orderId: 1 }`
- Tenant targeting, more cardinality, better splits
- Queries missing the leading field target poorly
- Leading field must match the important filter

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/44-compound.svg" alt="Compound tenant and orderId" width="720">

</div>
</div>

- **Do:** For equality queries, range queries, sequential writes, geographic locality, even distribution, and operational complexity, mark which strategy is usually stronger (or “depends”).

- **Expected:** History: ranged compound `{ customerId: 1, createdAt: 1 }`. UUID equality-only: hashed (or ranged UUID if already random).

## Exercise 7.11 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 7.11`](../slide-exercises/module-07/exercise-7.11-diagnose-hotspot-risks.md)

**Step 1 — Name the hotspot**
- **Do:** For timestamp shard key; dominant tenant; low-cardinality status; region zones with 90% of users in one region; celebrity product receiving most traffic — state what becomes hot.

- **Do:** Write one mitigation per case (hashed key, compound key, isolate tenant, split collection, cache, zone redesign, or not sharding that collection).
- **Expected:** Timestamp → hash or compound with high-cardinality leading field. Dominant tenant → isolate or further shard inside tenant. Status → do not use as key. Region s
