# The Balancer

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Redistributes ranges across shards
- Responds to uneven data, new shards, zones
- Consumes resources — monitor it
- Can be a surprise I/O storm if ignored

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/47-balancer.svg" alt="Balancer moving ranges" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Targeted Queries

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Enough shard-key information to pick shard(s)
- Example: customerId + orderNumber when customerId leads the key
- Usually less network, less merge, lower latency

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/49-targeted.svg" alt="mongos contacting one shard" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Scatter-Gather Queries

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Sent to many or all shards, then merged
- More network, latency, shard CPU, merge work
- Not always avoidable — keep them off the hot path

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/50-scatter-gather.svg" alt="Query fanning out to all shards" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Shard-Key Queries

| Query includes | Routing behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Full shard key | Usually targeted |
| Leading fields of a compound ranged key | May target selected ranges |
| Non-shard-key fields only | Often scatter-gather |
| Broad shard-key range | May hit multiple shards |
| Hashed key equality | Targeted |
| Hashed key range | Usually broadly distributed |

Exact routing depends on metadata and predicates.

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 7.9`](../slide-exercises/module-07/exercise-7.9-targeted-or-scatter-gather.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Assume ranged `{ customerId: 1, createdAt: 1 }`**
- **Do:** Classify: (A) `{ customerId: C101._id }`, (B) `{ customerId: C101._id, createdAt: { $gte: start } }`, (C) `{ paymentStatus: "PAID" }`, (D) `{ createdAt: { $gte: start } }`, (E) hashed-key range on `createdAt` if the key
- **Expected:** A targeted (one or few chunks for that customer). B targeted range within the customer prefix. C scatter-gather. D multi-shard or scatter depending on how dates

**Step 2 — Name one redesign**
- **Do:** If monthly global revenue must stay fast, is a better shard key the fix, or a different reporting design?
- **Expected:** Usually a different design: pre-aggregated reports, an analytics replica/cluster, or accepting scatter-gather for a rare job — not a shard key that hurts the OL

- Causes: monotonic keys, dominant tenants, skew, bad routing, zones, recent-data concentration

# Distributed Writes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Client → `mongos` → destination shard primary
- That replica set replicates the oplog
- Ack follows write concern
- Sharding and replication share the write path

</div>

# Unique Constraints in Sharded Collections

Unique indexes on sharded collections need the uniqueness pattern to be compatible with the shard key.

Design business identifiers **together** with the shard key when global uniqueness is required.

Confirm version- and deployment-specific rules before a production unique index. Do not assume `orderNumber` unique works the same as on a replica set.

# Transactions in Sharded Clusters

Multi-document transactions can span shards. Cost:

- Extra network and coordination
- Higher latency and failure complexity
- More resource use

Good modeling and shard keys reduce **unnecessary** cross-shard transactions. Prefer single-document or single-shard updates when the domain allows.

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Resharding Concepts

Workloads evolve. A key that once distributed well may hotspot or scatter later.

Resharding changes distribution to a new key. It is a major operational activity: capacity, compatibility, monitoring, performance tests, failure and rollback planning.

Choosing carefully the first time is cheaper than resharding under pressure.

# Sharding Operational Practices

- Choose keys from measured workload
- Replica sets for shards; redundant `mongos`
- Protect config servers
- Monitor routing, distribution, balancer
- Test shard failure
- Avoid uncontrolled scatter-gather on the hot path
- Back up the **distributed** deployment

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Sharded-Cluster Failure Scenarios

**One shard member fails** — the shard replica set may stay available if it keeps a primary.

**Shard loses primary** — operations that need that shard wait on election.

**One `mongos` fails** — clients use another router if configured.

**Config-server problems** — metadata and management suffer; this is serious.

## Lab 7.8 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Lab 7.8`](../slide-exercises/module-07/lab-7.8-analyze-query-routing.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Full shard-key equality**
- **Do:** On the sharded training collection, run `explain` for a find that includes the full shard key (or leading equality + range the instructor specifies). Record `shards` / `winningPlan` targeting.
- **Expected:** The plan indicates one (or a small set of) targeted shards, not all shards, when the key is present.

**Step 2 — Non-shard-key equality**
- **Do:** Explain a find on `paymentStatus` (or another non-key field) only. Record whether mongos scatters.
- **Expected:** Scatter-gather / query all shards is expected.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Expected: The plan indicates one (or a small set of) targeted shards, not all shards, when the key is present.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Do: Explain a find on paymentStatus (or another non-key field) only. Record whether mongos scatters.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Expected: Scatter-gather / query all shards is expected.

## Lab 7.8 — Steps 3–4

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 3 — Partial compound key and global aggregation**
- **Do:** Explain a filter that uses only the trailing field of a compound key, and a simple `$count` / `$group` with no shard-key `$match`. Record merge behavior.
- **Expected:** Trailing-only predicates usually cannot target. Aggregations without a targeted `$match` merge across shards.

**Step 4 — Summarize for the app team**
- **Do:** Write which of the five query shapes (full key, key range, partial compound, non-key, global agg) must stay rare in the hot path.
- **Expected:** Non-key finds and global aggregations are called out as expensive when frequent.

# Replication and Sharding Together

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Sharding partitions the data
- Replication copies each partition
- Each shard handles part of the data
- Each replica set protects its shard

</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Common Architecture Mistakes

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Treating replication as sharding — or sharding as backup
- Low-cardinality or monotonic ranged keys without analysis
- Ignoring routing; dumping all reports on secondaries
- Arbiter as a 'copy'; single-host URIs; ignoring write concern
- Adding shards before fixing schema and indexes

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-07/56-mistakes.svg" alt="Common mistakes" width="720">

</div>
</div>

## Exercise 7.12 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 7.12`](../slide-exercises/module-07/exercise-7.12-design-a-scalable-deployment.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Availability and placement**
- **Do:** Specify replica-set size, failure-domain placement, and how Canada vs Europe data-residency could be met (zones vs separate clusters). Assume 24/7 order writes.
- **Expected:** At least three data-bearing voters across failure domains. Residency: zoned sharding on a residency field **or** separate regional clusters — not an afterthough

**Step 2 — Orders versus products**
- **Do:** State which collection you shard first, a candidate order shard key, which queries stay targeted, and which monthly global reports become scatter-gather.
- **Expected:** Orders first under write growth. Products often wait. Targeted: customer/tenant order history. Scatter-gather: monthly global revenue unless pre-aggregated.

# Module Summary

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Replication: redundancy and failover via the oplog
- Sharding: distribute data and work via a shard key
- Writes go to a primary; elections need majority
- Preference, concern, and write concern are different knobs
- Targeted queries beat frequent scatter-gather
- Production shards are replica sets

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

# Module Knowledge Check

1. Main purpose of replication? Of sharding?
2. Primary vs secondary? What is the oplog?
3. What causes an election? Why majority?
4. What is replication lag?
5. Read preference vs read concern vs write concern?
6. Role of `mongos`? What do config servers store?
7. What is a shard key? Why is low cardinality a problem?
8. Why can a monotonic ranged key hotspot?
9. Ranged vs hashed? Targeted vs scatter-gather?
10. Why is each production shard a replica set?
11. Is replication a backup? Shard before fixing indexes?

# Exercise 7.13 — Scale the E-Commerce Order Platform

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

# From Functional to Production-Ready

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Functional:** connects, stores, queries, returns rows
- **Production-ready also:**
- Secure · available · scalable
- Observable · recoverable · tested
- Documented · maintainable · cost-aware
- **Key:** correctness is only one requirement

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/02-functional-vs-prod.svg" alt="Functional versus production-ready" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Data Modeling Best Practices

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Begin with access patterns
- Keep related bounded data together
- Separate independent or unbounded data
- Use intentional duplication
- Preserve historical snapshots
- Consistent names and types
- Validate critical expectations
- Review document size and array growth

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/01-module-map.svg" alt="Modeling sits inside production readiness" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Design Around Access Patterns

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Most frequent reads and writes
- Latency-sensitive operations
- Filter, sort, and returned fields
- Data retrieved together
- Expected growth and retention
- Avoid application-side joins on the hot path

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/04-access-patterns.svg" alt="Access-pattern checklist per collection" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Choose Document Boundaries Carefully

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- One business aggregate
- One ownership boundary
- One lifecycle
- One common read unit
- One atomic update boundary
- Orders embed items and snapshots; customers stay separate

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/05-document-boundary.svg" alt="Order aggregate versus customer master" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Embedding and Referencing Guidelines

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Embed when** owned, retrieved together, small and bounded, changes with the parent, atomicity matters
- **Reference when** unbounded, independent lifecycle, queried alone, widely shared, or would bloat the parent

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/06-embed-vs-ref.svg" alt="Embed versus reference decision table" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 2 on the slide: Reference when unbounded, independent lifecycle, queried alone, widely shared, or would bloat the parent.

The figure on this slide is titled: Embed versus reference decision table.

<!-- _class: split -->

# Bound Arrays and Document Growth

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Avoid arrays that grow forever
- Risky: all transactions, reviews, events, audits, logins
- Safer: separate collections, bucketing, subsets, archive, time partitions, retention

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/07-unbounded.svg" alt="Move unbounded reviews off the product" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Use Consistent Field Names and Types

Avoid mixing:

```javascript
{ price: Decimal128("49.99") }
{ productPrice: "49.99" }
{ item_cost: 49.99 }
```

Standardize naming, capitalization, dates, money, identifiers, statuses, nulls, and nesting.

Consistency improves queries, validation, indexes, and application code.

<!--

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Apply Schema Validation

Use `$jsonSchema` (and related rules) to enforce:

- Required identifiers
- Correct BSON types
- Allowed status values
- Nonnegative amounts
- Nested and array-element shape
- Valid dates

Protect invariants without blocking legitimate evolution — `warn` during migration, then `error`.

<!-- _class: split -->

# Plan for Schema Evolution

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Add compatible optional fields first
- Update readers before writers when you can
- Version documents if the shape forks
- Migrate history progressively
- Monitor mixed-schema documents
- Remove obsolete fields only after a dependency review
- Test validator changes before enforcement

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/08-schema-evolution.svg" alt="Compatible evolution then tighter validation" width="720">

</div>
</div>

- Status-change timestamps

<!-- _class: split -->

# Avoid Common Schema Anti-Patterns

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Copying relational tables into collections
- Unbounded arrays and oversized documents
- Inconsistent types and excessive nesting
- Uncontrolled duplication
- Unrelated entities in one collection — or too many tiny collections
- Modeling without access patterns
- Money as approximate floats or unplanned strings

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

# Query Design Best Practices

- Use selective filters and correct BSON types
- Prefer indexed fields for recurring shapes
- Return only required documents and fields
- Sort deterministically; limit and paginate
- Avoid uncontrolled regular expressions
- Inspect important query plans

<!--
This slide lists key points under Query Design Best Practices.

The slide title is: Query Design Best Practices.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Use selective filters and correct BSON types.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Prefer indexed fields for recurring shapes.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Return only required documents and fields.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Sort deterministically; limit and paginate.

Bullet 5 on the slide: Avoid uncontrolled regular expressions.

Bullet 6 on the slide: Inspect important query plans.
-->

---



<!-- _class: split -->

# Retrieve Only Required Documents

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Avoid `db.orders.find({})` when you need one customer’s paid orders
- Prefer `customerId` + `paymentStatus: "PAID"`
- Precise filters cut server work, network, client memory, and app CPU

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/11-selective-filter.svg" alt="Selective filter versus collection scan" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The figure on this slide is titled: Selective filter versus collection scan.
-->

---



<!-- _class: split -->

# Return Only Required Fields

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Project `orderNumber`, `fulfillmentStatus`, `total`, `createdAt`
- Drop `_id` when the client does not need it
- Projection matters most when documents hold large arrays or embeds

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/12-projection.svg" alt="Projection shrinks the payload" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 3 on the slide: Projection matters most when documents hold large arrays or embeds.

The figure on this slide is titled: Projection shrinks the payload.
-->

---



<!-- _class: split -->

# Use Appropriate BSON Types

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Timestamps → Date
- Exact money → Decimal128
- Flags → Boolean
- Quantities → integer types
- Ids → ObjectId or a consistent business id
- Wrong types break filters, sorts, math, and indexes

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/13-bson-types.svg" alt="BSON types for common fields" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Avoid Expensive Query Patterns

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Leading-wildcard or unanchored regex
- Large skip-based pagination
- Broad negative filters
- Missing shard-key predicates
- Huge result sets and app-side joins
- Sorts without a supporting index
- Examining far more documents than you return

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/14-expensive.svg" alt="Expensive query pattern grid" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Aggregation Pipeline Best Practices

- Start from the correct collection
- Filter early when the logic allows
- Build one stage at a time and inspect output
- Control array expansion
- Avoid unnecessary `$lookup`
- Handle null and missing values
- Validate calculations on a tiny sample
- Shape the final output; review the plan

<!--
This slide lists key points under Aggregation Pipeline Best Practices.

The slide title is: Aggregation Pipeline Best Practices.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Start from the correct collection.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Filter early when the logic allows.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Build one stage at a time and inspect output.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Control array expansion.

Bullet 5 on the slide: Avoid unnecessary $lookup.

Bullet 6 on the slide: Handle null and missing values.

Bullet 7 on the slide: Validate calculations on a tiny sample.

Bullet 8 on the slide: Shape the final output; review the plan.
-->

---



<!-- _class: split -->

# Reduce Pipeline Input Early

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Large collection → selective `$match` → smaller working set → expensive stages
- `$match` after `$group` filters grouped results — different job
- Early filters reduce work in `$unwind`, `$lookup`, and `$group`

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/15-early-match.svg" alt="Filter before expensive stages" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!--
This slide includes a diagram — Reduce Pipeline Input Early.

The slide title is: Reduce Pipeline Input Early.

The slide says: <div class="cols">.

The slide says: <div class="col-text">.

The slide says: </div>.

The slide says: <div class="col-visual">.

Bullet 1 on the slide: Large collection → selective $match → smaller working set → expensive stages.

Bullet 2 on the slide: $match after $group filters grouped results — different job.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Early filters reduce work in $unwind, $lookup, and $group.

The figure on this slide is titled: Filter before expensive stages.
-->

---



<!-- _class: split -->

# Control `$unwind` Expansion

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- 100,000 orders × 10 items → 1,000,000 documents
- Before unwind: filter, drop unused fields, confirm the array is required
- Estimate the expansion factor
- Do not sum parent totals after unwind

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/16-unwind.svg" alt="Unwind multiplies document count" width="720">

</div>
</div>

The figure on this slide is titled: Unwind multiplies document count.

<!-- _class: split -->

# Use `$lookup` Deliberately

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Is the data already embedded on purpose?
- Is the join required for this request?
- Is the foreign field indexed?
- How many matches? Will it create a large array?
- Can the foreign pipeline filter and project?
- Hot path versus occasional report?

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/17-lookup.svg" alt="Questions before adding lookup" width="720">

</div>

# Indexing Best Practices

- Index recurring query shapes
- Use compound indexes deliberately
- Start from Equality–Sort–Range
- Review prefixes; measure with `explain()`
- Hide before you drop; monitor usage
- Account for write and storage cost
- Revisit indexes as the workload changes

# Balance Read and Write Performance

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Extra indexes can speed selected reads
- They add insert, update, delete work
- Plus storage, RAM, replication traffic, backup size
- The portfolio must match the whole workload

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/20-index-cost.svg" alt="Index benefit versus write cost" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<div class="cols">

- A compound index may already cover a shorter prefix
- Before removal: review workload, explain, hide, monitor, drop with rollback

# MongoDB Security Principles

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Identity, authentication, authorization
- Network isolation, encryption, secret protection
- Auditing, patching, backups, monitoring
- No single control is enough

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/23-security-layers.svg" alt="Layered MongoDB security controls" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Authentication

Authentication verifies identity.

Sources may include database users, certificates, enterprise identity, cloud identity, and workload identities.

Avoid shared admin accounts, default or weak passwords, anonymous access, and long-lived secrets without rotation.

<!--
Let's look at Authentication.

The slide title is: Authentication.

The slide says: Authentication verifies identity.

The slide says: Sources may include database users, certificates, enterprise identity, cloud identity, and workload identities.

The slide says: Avoid shared admin accounts, default or weak passwords, anonymous access, and long-lived secrets without rotation.
-->

---



<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Authorization and Role-Based Access

Authorization decides permitted operations:

- Read or read/write application data
- Manage indexes
- Inspect monitoring
- Administer users and backups
- Administer the cluster

Roles should match responsibilities — not job titles copied from email.

Bullet 5 on the slide: Administer the cluster.
-->

---



<!-- _class: split -->

# Principle of Least Privilege

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Grant only what the workload needs
- App: readWrite on its database
- Reporting: read on approved collections
- Backup and monitoring: their own roles
- Never put clusterAdmin in application code

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/24-least-privilege.svg" alt="Least-privilege identity ceiling" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Network Security

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Private networks, firewalls, allowlists
- Segmentation and controlled admin paths
- No unnecessary public exposure
- Separate application and management access
- Review rules continuously

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/25-network.svg" alt="Private network then allowlist" width="720">

</div>
</div>

# Encryption in Transit and at Rest

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **Transit (TLS):** app, admins, replica members, shard components, backup paths
- Validate certificates — encryption without identity checks is weak
- **At rest:** disks, snapshots, backups, temp files, exports, logs
- Pair with key management and access policy

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/26-encryption.svg" alt="TLS in transit and encryption at rest" width="720">

# Application Credential Management

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Do not store secrets in source, images, screenshots, shared docs, or open config files
- Use a secret manager, protected injection, workload identity
- Rotate, separate environments, audit access

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/27-secrets.svg" alt="Secrets stay out of source control" width="720">

</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Data Classification and Sensitive Fields

Classify PII, payment data, tokens, health, financial, and confidential business fields.

Then define who may access them, where they live, how long they stay, masking, field-level protection, and audit.

Do not put password hashes on orders. Do not copy production dumps to intern laptops.

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Auditing and Security Logging

Log authentication success/failure, user and role changes, admin and config operations, collection changes, sensitive access, backup and restore.

Protect logs from tampering and from leaking the secrets they might contain.

# Secure Configuration Practices

- Enable authentication; restrict bindings; encrypt connections
- Least-privilege roles; disable unnecessary exposure
- Rotate secrets; separate dev, test, and production
- Patch; protect backups; review config changes
- Keep an asset and owner inventory

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Public database port; authentication off
- Shared administrator credentials
- Secrets in source control; no TLS
- App running as cluster admin
- Dev accounts in production
- Unprotected backups; secrets in logs
- No monitoring or access review

</div>

## Exercise 8.6 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 8.6`](../slide-exercises/module-08/exercise-8.6-design-least-privilege-roles.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Fill the permission matrix**
- **Do:** For each identity — application service, reporting service, support engineer, monitoring service, backup service, database administrator — list one permitted operation and one prohibited operation on `training_store`.
- **Expected:** App: read/write app collections, not userAdmin. Reporting: read approved collections, not update. Support: read (maybe limited PII), not drop. Monitoring: clust

**Step 2 — Call out the anti-pattern**
- **Do:** Write two sentences on why the application must not use a cluster-administrator account, even in training-like environments that later become production.
- **Expected:** A stolen app credential would inherit every privilege. Least privilege limits blast radius and makes audit trails meaningful.

# Backup and Recovery Fundamentals

A strategy must define what, how often, where, protection, retention, restore steps, owner, and test cadence.

A backup is valuable only if it can be restored.

<!--
Let's look at Backup and Recovery Fundamentals.

The slide title is: Backup and Recovery Fundamentals.

The slide says: A strategy must define what, how often, where, protection, retention, restore steps, owner, and test cadence.

The slide says: A backup is valuable only if it can be restored.
-->

---



<!-- _class: split -->

# Replication vs. Backup

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Replication helps with server and some infrastructure failure and planned maintenance
- It does **not** independently protect against drops, malice, bad migrations, or slow corruption
- Mistakes replicate to every member

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/29-repl-vs-backup.svg" alt="Replica sets versus backups" width="720">

</div>
</div>

Bullet 1 on the slide: Replication helps with server and some infrastructure failure and planned maintenance.

Bullet 2 on the slide: It does not independently protect against drops, malice, bad migrations, or slow corruption.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Mistakes replicate to every member.

The figure on this slide is titled: Replica sets versus backups.
-->

---



<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Backup Strategy

Combine as the platform allows:

- Scheduled snapshots and/or continuous backup
- Point-in-time recovery
- Logical exports for subsets or migration
- Offsite or separate-account storage
- Retention, encryption, restore testing, named owners

<!--
This slide lists key points under Backup Strategy.

The slide title is: Backup Strategy.

The slide says: Combine as the platform allows:.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Point-in-time recovery.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Logical exports for subsets or migration.

Bullet 4 on the slide: Offsite or separate-account storage.

Bullet 5 on the slide: Retention, encryption, restore testing, named owners.
-->

---



<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Logical vs. Physical Backup

| Logical | Physical |
|---------|----------|
| Exports database content | Copies files or snapshots |
| Portable subsets | Efficient full recovery |
| Slower at large scale | Needs compatible restore |
| Migration and selected data | Large deployments |

Choose from scale, RPO/RTO, and platform — not from habit.

<!-- _class: split -->

# Recovery Point and Recovery Time Objectives

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- **RPO:** maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (example: 15 minutes)
- **RTO:** maximum acceptable time to restore service (example: 2 hours)
- Backup frequency and restore design must beat those numbers

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/30-rpo-rto.svg" alt="RPO versus RTO" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: split -->

# Restore Testing

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Readable backup, credentials and keys, procedure, duration
- Data consistency, app connectivity, indexes, users/roles
- Documentation that someone else can follow
- Successful backup jobs do not prove recovery

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/31-restore-test.svg" alt="Restore test goes beyond a green job" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Point-in-Time Recovery and Disaster Recovery

**PITR** restores to a moment before a bad drop, deploy, bulk update, or app corruption — if the platform kept history.

A DR plan names scenarios, architecture, backup location, region strategy, RPO/RTO, people, comms, app reconnect, validation, test schedule, and return-to-normal.

# Monitoring Fundamentals

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Is it up? Is it fast enough?
- Is workload or capacity changing?
- Is replication healthy? Is data balanced?
- Are backups succeeding?
- Are security events happening?
- Are users seeing errors?

</div>
<div class="col-visual">

<img src="assets/module-08/32-monitor.svg" alt="Questions a dashboard must answer" width="720">

</div>
</div>

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Database, Query, and Resource Metrics

**Health:** availability, op rates, latency, queues, connections, cache/working set, errors, data and index size.

**Queries:** slow ops, latency percentiles, examined vs returned, COLLSCAN, in-memory sorts, timeouts, heavy aggregations.

**Resources:** CPU, memory, disk capacity/latency/throughput, network, filesystem, container limits.

Symptoms often start in infrastructure, not in BSON.

<!--

The slide says: Queries: slow ops, latency percentiles, examined vs returned, COLLSCAN, in-memory sorts, timeouts, heavy aggregations.

The slide says: Resources: CPU, memory, disk capacity/latency/throughput, network, filesystem, container limits.

The slide says: Symptoms often start in infrastructure, not in BSON.
-->

---



<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Replication, Sharding, and Connection Metrics

**Replication:** primary, member health, lag, oplog window, elections, rollbacks, errors, secondary resource use.

**Sharding:** distribution, hot shards, mongos/CSRS health, balancer, migrations, targeted vs scatter-gather, zone compliance.

**Connections:** current, spawn rate, pool use, rejected, auth failures, leaks, sudden load.

Application pools must be sized on purpose.

# Logging Best Practices

Logs should be centralized, time-synced, searchable, access-controlled, retained, tamper-resistant, correlated with app and infra, and free of unnecessary secrets.

Useful fields: timestamp, component, host, severity, operation, error code, correlation id.

<div class="cols">
<div class="col-text">

- Define the symptom, users, start time, recent changes
- Collect metrics and logs; reproduce safely
- Isolate the layer; one hypothesis; one change
- Verify recovery; document cause and prevention

# Authentication and Authorization Troubleshooting

**Authentication failure:** username, password, auth source, certificate, expiry, URI encoding.

**Authorization failure:** roles, target database, operation, collection privileges, inheritance, recent grants/revokes.

A ping can succeed while inserts fail — that is authorization, not ‘Mongo is down’.

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Query, Aggregation, and Index Troubleshooting

**Query:** db/collection, case, nested paths, BSON types, filter logic, arrays, projection, sort, indexes, explain, result size.

**Aggregation:** shape, stage order, field paths, per-stage output, group keys, nulls, types, unwind multiplication, lookup types, double count, time zones.

**Index not used:** leading fields, predicates, sort direction, types, partial filter, collation, selectivity, multikey, projection, competing indexes, actual stats.

The slide says: Index not used: leading fields, predicates, sort direction, types, partial filter, collation, selectivity, multikey, projection, competing indexes, actual stats.
-->

<!-- _class: content fit-sm -->

# Replication, Sharding, and Capacity Troubleshooting

**Replication:** primary, majority, member health, network, lag, oplog window, disk/CPU, elections, write concern, recent config.

**Sharding:** mongos, CSRS, shard health, shard-key predicates, targeting, hot shards, balancer, zones, migrations, cross-shard ops.

**Capacity:** latency, queues, disk, memory, CPU, connections, storage. Cause may be growth, bad queries, missing or extra indexes, huge documents, infra limits, or maintenance.

## Exercise 8.11 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 8.11`](../slide-exercises/module-08/exercise-8.11-diagnose-an-operational-incident.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Form the hypothesis**
- **Do:** Evidence: CPU moderately up; documents examined up sharply; no election; connections normal; a query filter changed; indexes unchanged. What is the likely cause, and what is not the cause?
- **Expected:** Likely: the new filter no longer uses the existing index (predicate, type, or field name), causing a collection scan or a weakly selective plan. Not: failover, 

**Step 2 — Mitigate and prevent**
- **Do:** Write immediate mitigation, evidence to collect, permanent correction, and one prevention action for the next release.
- **Expected:** Mitigate: revert the filter or add a matching index if the new shape is intended. Collect: the exact query, explain before/after, deploy diff. Permanent: index

## Exercise 8.12 — Steps 1–2

**Lab guide:** [`Exercise 8.12`](../slide-exercises/module-08/exercise-8.12-create-an-operational-runbook.md)

**Follow along (Windows) — key steps:**

**Step 1 — Fill the template**
- **Do:** Pick one event. Write: alert name, meaning, business impact, required access, diagnostic commands, expected normal state, decision points, corrective actions, escalation, rollback, verification, and where the incident is
- **Expected:** A complete page exists. Diagnostics are real commands (`rs.status()`, `explain`, disk checks). Corrective actions are sequenced. Escalation has a person or role

**Step 2 — Add a verification step**
- **Do:** Write how you know the incident is over (metric + user-facing check) and what you will change so it does not recur silently.
- **Expected:** Example: primary exists for 15 minutes, checkout succeeds, lag < baseline. Follow-up: alert threshold, dashboard tile, or change-review item.

- **Expected:** Revenue is not multiplied by line count. Units come from item quantities. July–September 2026 months appear.
